Issue Reading note
One reportable segment Note 7 of the FY2025 accounts states the Group "continues to have one reportable segment" under IFRS 8. Oncology, BioPharmaceuticals and Rare Disease are disaggregated-revenue categories. No segment operating profit, no segment assets and no segment margin exists in any filing. Every franchise profitability figure in this dossier is tagged [estimate: method].
Core versus Reported FY2025 Reported operating profit was $13,743m (23.4% margin) against Core $18,478m (31.5%), a $4,735m gap of which $4,327m is intangible amortisation and impairment. Reported EPS $6.60, Core EPS $9.16. Guidance and consensus are Core-only. Never compare a Reported growth rate to a Core one.
FY2025 is six months stale; three things have since inflected Cardiovascular, Renal & Metabolism went +2% CER (FY2025) to −18% CER (Q2 2026) on Farxiga's US loss of exclusivity; China went +4% CER to −13% CER on volume-based procurement; and Oncology accelerated to 48% of Q2 2026 revenue at +15% CER.
Product Sales, Product Revenue and Total Revenue are three different bases Total Revenue = Product Sales + Alliance Revenue + Collaboration Revenue ($55,573m + $3,067m + $99m = $58,739m in FY2025). Beyfortus is $281m of Product Sales but $703m of Total Revenue; Enhertu is $977m of Product Sales with zero in the US, plus $1,798m of Alliance Revenue. Shares of "revenue" differ by basis for the same medicine.

The American Depositary Share programme was terminated on 2 February 2026 and Ordinary Shares were directly listed on the NYSE the same day, so any US price series before that date is an ADS series on a 2-for-1 ratio and is not spliceable to the current line. External-consensus framing comes from the Bloomberg terminal and from named published notes rather than from broker research.

1. Business description, model and unit economics

AstraZeneca discovers, develops, manufactures and sells patented prescription medicines in three therapy-area franchises. FY2025 Total Revenue was $58,739m, up 9% actual and 8% CER, from about 40 named medicines sold in more than 120 countries. The company employed 96,100 people at the end of 2025 and spent $14,232m on research and development, 24.2% of Total Revenue.

1.1 What sets price

AstraZeneca does not set the realised price to patients.▪ The US gross-to-net reconciliation is the only price series the company publishes.

Chargebacks (340B, GPO, VA/DoD, hospital) (3,075) (3,969) (5,113) +66.3%
Regulatory — Medicaid and state programmes (2,417) (2,184) (2,527) +4.6%
Contractual — managed care and Medicare (11,035) (10,825) (13,963) +26.5%
Cash and other discounts (428) (430) (483)
Customer returns (222) (111) (149)
US branded pharmaceutical fee (124) (114) (99)

Source: 20-F FY2025, "Gross to Net Product Sales — US pharmaceuticals". The FY2025 accrual carried forward was $5,941m and both the rate and the accrual are Key Judgements; PwC listed the managed-care, Medicaid and Medicare Part D rebate accrual excluding Rare Diseases as its first key audit matter against group materiality of $620m.

The deductions totalled $23,941m in FY2025 against a whole-group cost of sales of $10,633m, so they are 2.25x manufacturing cost.▪ Managed-care and Medicare rebates grew 29% in the year against 16.6% growth in gross sales, which is the Medicare Part D redesign and its 20% manufacturer liability. And chargebacks grew 66% over two years against 30% growth in gross sales, which is the 340B and government channel expanding faster than the commercial book.

The marginal dollar is worse than the average. Over 2022–2025 AstraZeneca added $15,285m of US gross Product Sales and kept $6,190m of it, a 40.5% marginal net capture against a 49.5% average; in FY2025 alone the marginal capture was 26.5%.▪

Realised price growth on the existing patient is between one and three percent a year. From CMS administrative data covering 2020–2024, gross price per dosage unit grew at +1.5% a year for Tagrisso, +2.8% for Lynparza, +1.8% for Imfinzi, +2.9% for Enhertu and −0.1% for Imjudo (CMS Medicare Part D and Part B Spending by Drug, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. Against US Oncology Product Sales compounding at 21.4% a year from 2020 to 2025, roughly 88–91% of the growth is volume and 9–12% is price.▪

Administered prices now move the other way on named products. Farxiga's Medicare Maximum Fair Price took effect on 1 January 2026 at $178.50 per 30-day supply, a 68% discount to the 2023 list price of $556 (cms.gov, accessed 2026-08-07) [web, unverified]. Calquence was selected in the second negotiation round with its Maximum Fair Price effective 1 January 2027 at $8,600 per 30-day supply, 41% below the $14,486 list price (Simon-Kucher, IPAY 2027 outcomes, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. US Calquence plus US Farxiga were $4,069m of FY2025 net US Product Sales, 17.4% of the US book, and both now have an administratively set price.▪

1.2 What drives unit volume, and the demand-driver tree

Volume decomposes into patients treated, days of therapy per patient and country count. AstraZeneca confirms it computes its own patient numbers the same way: "The number of patients treated by our medicines is estimated based on volume of inventory sold, assumed days of therapy and average level of patient adherence to the treatment" (FY2025 Annual Report, methodology note). The tree below goes through the drivers of revenue growth over the last three years.

Fixed-duration regimen design is described as a Calquence growth driver — "AMPLIFY continues to gain share in reimbursed markets… supported by the clear global trend towards adoption of finite duration treatments" (Q2 2026 call) — while a 14-cycle fixed course displaces treat-to-progression dosing and lowers lifetime revenue per patient. And partnered gross-profit share, at $1,875m of Oncology Total Revenue in FY2025 and the fastest-growing branch, is the dollar over which AstraZeneca has the least control: Daiichi Sankyo owns and manufactures Enhertu and Datroway, AstraZeneca books no US Enhertu Product Sales and holds no Datroway commercialisation rights.▪

The economic unit differs by franchise: one patient-day of therapy for the oral oncology medicines, one milligram of drug substance for infused biologics, and one patient-year for the chronic and ultra-orphan books.

Reconciliation to reported cost of sales. Group cost of sales was $10,633m in FY2025, 19.1% of Product Sales, of which $7,600m is inventories recognised as an expense (13.7% of Product Sales, disclosed at Note 16) and $3,033m is non-inventory: collaboration profit shares, royalties, a $235m royalty buyout on Saphnelo and rilvegostomig, an Alexion fair-value release and a restructuring credit. The per-unit costs above imply 3–6% of Product Sales for oncology manufacturing and 2–8% for BioPharmaceuticals, which does not reconcile to the 13.7% group inventory ratio. The reason is the composition of the other half of the portfolio. Group cost of sales is set by low-value-density primary-care volume, inhaler devices, the FluMist vaccine (which the CFO names as a lower-margin medicine) and cost-plus manufacture for Sanofi. Building Oncology's own cost of sales bottom-up gives roughly $3.2bn, about 12% of franchise Total Revenue and an implied Oncology gross margin near 88–89% [estimate: 4–6% manufacturing plus a 45–50% MSD share of Lynparza gross profit plus royalties], which puts the rest of the group at 76–78%, consistent with retail inhalers, statins and cost-plus manufacture.

Cost of sales is a fixed network plus contractual revenue shares. At the end of 2025 AstraZeneca employed 16,900 people at 31 Operations sites in 15 countries, with $879m of property, plant and equipment depreciation on a $12,962m net book value. None of that scales down when Farxiga's US volume disappears. So the incremental gross margin on new volume and the decremental margin on lost exclusivity revenue are both in the low-to-mid nineties [estimate: per-unit variable cost against realised price, franchise-scoped; the group cost-of-sales line is not the right denominator for this comparison and the reconciliation above explains why].

Oncology and Rare Disease keep most of their list price and BioPharmaceuticals gives most of it away.▪ Triangulating from CMS-visible gross spending against disclosed US net Product Sales puts each of the four large oncology medicines at a US gross-to-net deduction of 8–27%, centring near 15–20% [estimate: CMS administrative gross ÷ assumed public-payer share of US volume, cross-checked against list price]. Rare Disease is disclosed at 5.7% of the $5,941m US rebate accrual on 23.1% of US net Product Sales, and the auditors scope it out of the rebate key audit matter entirely, which implies a deduction near 20% (range 13–27%) [estimate: allocate the total US deduction by the disclosed Rare Disease share of the accrual]. The residual for BioPharmaceuticals plus Other Medicines is a deduction near 75%. That is the largest single economic difference between the three franchises.

1.4 Operating leverage

Realised incremental Core operating margins over the last three years are very close to average margins.

Window Δ Total Revenue $m Δ Core operating profit $m Incremental Core operating margin Core margin at the end
FY2022 → FY2025 14,388 5,128 35.6% 31.5%
FY2023 → FY2025 12,928 3,944 30.5% 31.5%
FY2024 → FY2025 4,666 1,550 33.2% 31.5%
H1 2025 → H1 2026 2,627 1,123 42.7% 34.3%

On $14.4bn of revenue added between FY2022 and FY2025 the Core operating margin moved 1.4 percentage points, from 30.1% to 31.5%. Indexed to revenue, the cost lines show where the leverage came from: selling, general and administrative expense declined from 47.9% of Total Revenue in FY2019 to 33.9% in FY2025, fourteen points, while research and development was 24.3% in FY2015 and 24.2% in FY2025, flat for a decade. Every point of margin expansion has been commercial-cost dilution against a bigger revenue base; none has come from research efficiency.▪

H1 2026 is the first period in which the incremental margin rose sharply, driven by mix, not scale.▪ What left was primary-care revenue at a 92–98% contribution margin (Farxiga −11% CER, Brilinta −66%, roxadustat −64%); what arrived was Oncology at +15% CER and Rare Disease at +11%. Gross margin went 82% (FY2025) to 83% (H1 2026) to 84% (Q2 2026) while Oncology's share of Total Revenue went 43.6% to 46% to 48%.▪

Capital intensity is stepping up, and the spend is for Oncology and weight management. Purchases of property, plant and equipment went from $1,091m in FY2022 to $2,810m in FY2025, 2.5% to 4.8% of revenue. The $50bn announced US manufacturing and research programme includes a $4.5bn drug-substance plant at Charlottesville, Virginia for the weight-management and antibody-drug-conjugate portfolios, $2bn in Maryland, an expanded Coppell, Texas site and a $1.5bn antibody-drug-conjugate plant in Singapore. Management guides FY2026 capital expenditure up about one third on FY2025's $3,270m base including capitalised software. Working capital does not fund growth: inventory days were 225 on cost of sales in FY2025 and the cash conversion cycle 188 days, and the US rebate accrual reverses when a product goes generic (Section 5.4) — the CFO attributed part of the 12% H1 2026 decline in operating cash flow to "working capital impact associated with U.S. loss of exclusivity for Forxiga" and said the effect persists through the second half.

2. Key technologies and technical differentiators

What excludes competitors from a specific medicine is composition-of-matter and formulation patents with their extensions, regulatory data and orphan exclusivity, the clinical evidence base a rival must beat, and the commercial and manufacturing scale to launch everywhere at once.▪

The DXd antibody-drug conjugate platform (licensed from Daiichi Sankyo) differentiates, and AstraZeneca does not own it. An antibody-drug conjugate joins a targeting antibody to a cytotoxic payload through a linker; the design problem is that a linker which releases payload in circulation delivers chemotherapy to the whole body, which caps the dose.▪ The Daiichi Sankyo chemistry uses a tetrapeptide linker cleaved only by lysosomal proteases with an exatecan-derivative payload at a drug-to-antibody ratio near 4:1. AstraZeneca's own description of the consequence: "What's different about Dato-DXd is it's got a highly plasma-stable linker. This is supported by its half-life of 5 days compared to other TROP2 ADCs that have less than 1 day half-life" (WCLC 2024 investor call, 9 September 2024). The external literature supports the comparison — sacituzumab govitecan uses a hydrolysable linker with a plasma half-life of roughly 11–15 hours, while the preclinical terminal half-life of datopotamab deruxtecan in primates was 45.1 ± 13.9 hours (AACR Mol Cancer Ther, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. Lower bone-marrow toxicity is what permits combination with platinum chemotherapy and checkpoint inhibitors.

Enhertu is standard of care in HER2-positive and HER2-low metastatic breast cancer, holds the first HER2-directed tumour-agnostic approval, is approved in more than 90 countries and generated $2,775m of AstraZeneca Total Revenue in FY2025 at +40% CER. Datroway generated $78m five years after a deal with $1bn of upfront payments and up to $6bn of total consideration: TROPION-Lung01 missed statistical significance on final overall survival against docetaxel (14.6 against 12.3 months median in the non-squamous subgroup, hazard ratio 0.84, 95% confidence interval 0.68–1.05, not alpha-controlled), the US and EU applications in advanced non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer were withdrawn in November 2024 and a narrower accelerated-approval filing substituted. Meanwhile Merck & Co. and Kelun-Biotech's sacituzumab tirumotecan reported a 65% reduction in risk of progression or death against Keytruda alone in treatment-naive PD-L1-positive non-small-cell lung cancer — a planned interim analysis in a China-only trial with overall survival not mature — and met primary endpoints in three further Phase III settings; Gilead's Trodelvy received a PD-L1-agnostic first-line triple-negative breast cancer US label in June 2026 (FiercePharma, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. Pascal Soriot predicted this at the 2024 Investor Day: "the rate of replacement of products in those — coming from this technology is going to accelerate, especially with China coming on board… if we are not experts in those technologies in the long run, I think we'll progressively lose ground."

AstraZeneca's own antibody-drug conjugate platform has no Phase III data. Eight wholly owned conjugates are in the clinic and three in Phase III. Management stated at JPM 2026 that puxitatug samrotecan and torvutatug samrotecan are "the first ADCs to move into Phase III using AstraZeneca's proprietary linker payload technology", and separately that CLARITY-Gastric01 is "the first Phase III data from our wholly owned ADC portfolio". Both are true only because sonesitatug vedotin uses monomethyl auristatin E, the industry-standard payload, not AstraZeneca chemistry (20-F: "CLDN18.2 MMAE ADC"). The proprietary platform's first readout is dated 2027, and the $1.5bn Singapore plant is being built ahead of any wholly owned conjugate revenue.▪

Next-generation immuno-oncology bispecifics are the largest single technology bet and every readout is 2027 or later. Rilvegostomig binds PD-1 and TIGIT; volrustomig binds PD-1 and CTLA-4. The stated intent is displacement of the company's own franchise: "the real big challenge that we are taking here is to replace PD-1 and PD-L1 inhibitors with our bispecifics" (Investor Day 2024). Imfinzi was $6,063m of FY2025 Product Sales, so the franchise being defended and the franchise being replaced are the same one.▪ TIGIT is the highest-profile failed target in immuno-oncology — Roche's tiragolumab and Merck's vibostolimab both failed in Phase III — and AstraZeneca's answer is patient selection by PD-L1 expression rather than a claim of a chemically different molecule, which is a trial-design bet. The 20-F pipeline table lists nine rilvegostomig Phase III rows, eight dated 2027 or later, against management counts of 14 and then 16 ongoing Phase III trials that cannot be reconciled to the table.

Complement inhibition still generates the returns and is losing its monopoly on the indications. Terminal C5 inhibition blocks membrane-attack-complex formation, stopping intravascular haemolysis in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and complement damage at the neuromuscular junction in generalised myasthenia gravis. Ultomiris is an engineered variant of the same antibody with recycling modifications that extend dosing from two weeks to eight, which is a convenience improvement rather than a new mechanism. Ultomiris was $4,718m in FY2025 at +19% CER, decelerating to +14% CER in H1 2026 and +12% in Q2. Against that, argenx's FcRn blocker Vyvgart — a different mechanism, lowering circulating immunoglobulin G rather than inhibiting complement — reported "$4.2 billion in full year 2025 product net sales, representing 90% year-over-year growth" and 19,000 patients globally (argenx FY2025 results, accessed 2026-08-07) [web], and Novartis's oral Factor B inhibitor Fabhalta reached $505m at +291%. Gefurulimab, AstraZeneca's once-weekly self-administered nanobody, answers Vyvgart's subcutaneous format but is a delivery advantage inside a mechanism under attack.

The inhaled propellant transition is the clearest dated competitive advantage in the portfolio. Current pressurised metered-dose inhalers use HFA-134a, with a global warming potential near 1,430. AstraZeneca committed $500m in 2020 to replace it with HFO-1234ze(E), near-zero global warming potential, and established bioequivalence for reformulated Breztri and Trixeo. The MHRA approved Trixeo Aerosphere with the new propellant in May 2025 as the first inhaled respiratory medicine using one; the nearest competitor, Chiesi, obtained MHRA approval for HFA-152a inhalers on 21 July 2026 (European Pharmaceutical Review, accessed 2026-08-07) [web], roughly 14 months later and on a chemistry with a global warming potential of 124 against near zero. Propellant emissions are 26% of AstraZeneca's total Scope 3 footprint, so in health systems that ration by carbon footprint the transition is a commercial defence as much as a climate one — GSK's respiratory franchise is dry-powder-weighted and does not have the same problem.▪ Chiesi markets HFA-152a as free of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, and HFO-1234ze is a hydrofluoroolefin, so a European restriction on that chemistry forces a second reformulation.

Enzyme replacement is excellent economics from market structure, not from technology. Strensiq was $1,678m in FY2025 at +19% CER and $1,053m in H1 2026 at +40% CER on an enzyme approved in 2015. Hypophosphatasia has no competing approved product and a population of about 11,500 diagnosed patients across the top eight countries, so the exclusion mechanism is orphan status plus the practical impossibility of recruiting a competing trial.▪

Antisense, radioconjugates, cell therapy and subcutaneous reformulation are licensed capabilities without revenue. Wainua (licensed from Ionis) was $212m and its large indication failed: CARDIO-TTRansform in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy did not meet its primary endpoint in July 2026, while Alnylam's Amvuttra won that indication. The Fusion radioconjugate platform cost $2,195m in June 2024 and is Phase I/II with zero revenue, against a supply constraint the filings do not address at all (Section 18). On subcutaneous delivery AstraZeneca licenses hyaluronidases from Alteogen and Halozyme; Merck's subcutaneous Keytruda Qlex was approved in September 2025, generated $463m in Q2 2026 alone and is targeted at 30–40% adoption by end-2027, so the exposure is timing rather than technology.

Artificial intelligence: one asset passes the differentiation test. More than 90% of small-molecule discovery is described as AI-enabled; MILTON integrates de-identified health records with genetic data to predict risk for more than 1,000 diseases; an agentic development system is claimed to have "potential to decrease time to commercial scale up for synthetic manufacturing by up to 50%"; digital changeover is deployed across 17 sites. Every one of those is an input metric. Quantitative Continuous Scoring is different. TROP2 is post-translationally cleaved, so standard immunohistochemistry cannot predict conjugate benefit and only the internalised membrane-to-cytoplasm ratio can. The method has an FDA Breakthrough Device Designation for an AI-driven companion diagnostic developed with Roche Tissue Diagnostics. Its retrospective efficacy support is a response rate of 36.8% against 15.3% for docetaxel in biomarker-positive non-squamous patients and a progression-free survival hazard ratio of 0.57. Its prospective test is AVANZAR in H2 2026, where the cut point was optimised retrospectively on TROPION-Lung01. The external base rates are unhelpful: AI-discovered molecules achieve 80–90% Phase I success but only about 40% in Phase II, in line with history, and roughly $60bn has flowed into AI drug discovery since 2019 producing about 175 clinical-stage programmes and no approvals (IntuitionLabs, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. None of the transformative platforms contributes to the 2030 revenue case.▪ Of 108 dated rows in the FY2025 20-F Phase III, pivotal Phase II and registration table, 48 (44%) read out in 2027 or later, and 24 of those are conjugate, bispecific, T-cell-engager, cell-therapy or radioconjugate programmes against 7 such rows reading out in 2026. Asked at JPM 2026 what underpins growth beyond 2030, the CFO said of the assets on the 2027 readout list that many "actually don't reach their peak sales" inside the window and contribute little to the $80bn. The three named 2026 launches — baxdrostat, camizestrant and gefurulimab — are a small molecule and two conventional biologics.

3. Competitive advantages and moat assessment

AstraZeneca earns returns above its cost of capital today, driven by a portfolio of patent monopolies, scale in trial execution, and distribution.▪ Core return on invested capital was 21.0% in FY2025 against a 7–8% cost of capital. In every class where a well-funded rival attacked with better clinical data, AstraZeneca lost the lead or never held it. The erosion is already in the reported numbers.

Gross margin was 81.9% in FY2025 against a peer median of 74.8%, a 7.1-point premium that has been stable for six years and widened to 83.6% in Q2 2026 as cost of sales grew 3% CER against 5% revenue growth.▪ Oncology's identifiable book capital is small relative to its earnings — roughly $12.3bn of product intangibles against $25.6bn of revenue [estimate: Note 11 named significant assets assigned by franchise, unnamed residual pro-rated] — because Tagrisso, Imfinzi, Lynparza and Truqap were discovered internally and their development cost was expensed, never capitalised. And Oncology now supplies all of the group's growth: 70% of group revenue growth in FY2025, 82% in H1 2026 and 109% in Q2 2026, the last of those meaning the rest of AstraZeneca shrank.▪

Switching costs on new patients are close to zero. BeOne Medicines' zanubrutinib passed Calquence in quarterly revenue in Q4 2024 and has widened the gap since: BRUKINSA $3,900m in FY2025 at +49% against Calquence's $3,518m at +12% CER, and $2,800m of US revenue against $2,339m, with BeOne stating BRUKINSA holds more than 50% of US new-patient share in all lines of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (BeOne FY2025 results; FiercePharma, both accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. Same mechanism, same indications, same payers, same specialty channel, both companies well funded. Calquence still grew 16% CER in Q2 2026 and crossed $1bn in a quarter for the first time: with zero switching cost and a slow-decaying installed base, the incumbent keeps its existing patients and loses the new ones.▪

The largest medicine is under direct scientific attack. Johnson & Johnson's MARIPOSA trial "met the final pre-specified secondary endpoint of OS and demonstrated clinically meaningful and statistically significant improvement in OS versus the current standard of care osimertinib" in first-line EGFR-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer, with 56% of combination patients alive at 3.5 years against 44% (J&J press release, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. Tagrisso's CER growth decelerated from +10% (FY2025) to +8% (H1 2026) to +6% (Q2 2026). Management named the two threats itself on the Q2 2026 call — "the multiplicity of EGFR in [the China] market, and… the Mariposa regimen" — and states that US share has held so far: "on MARIPOSA, we have not seen any impact… on U.S. Tagrisso shares" (Q1 2026 call). Both statements can be true; an overall-survival win that has not yet converted is still a win. The company's response was to license a rival molecule, paying Dizal $600m upfront plus up to $900m of milestones plus tiered royalties for Zegfrovy in July 2026, framed as "a clear signal of our intent to remain the definitive leader in this space".▪

The gross-margin premium is spent on research. Research and development was 24.2% of Total Revenue in FY2025, the highest of the large-cap group except Merck, Regeneron and Vertex, so Reported operating margin of 23.4% was 5.3 points below the peer median of 28.7% and Reported return on invested capital of 15.6% was 6.1 points below the peer median of 21.7%.▪

Management claims: portfolio breadth enabling combinations. Soriot on the Q2 2026 call: "The ability we have to combine products through our portfolio to defend our various franchises and build beyond where we are… we are really reducing the space where the competition could actually have an impact over time." At the 2024 Investor Day the same argument was put at the centre: "cure in oncology will require a combination… we can actually displace chemo-pembro with a combination of ADCs with IO." The closest management comes to naming a mechanism is a claim about outspending rivals: "there's very much a correlation between investment in R&D and oncology and success commercially within oncology… we've been steadily increasing our investment in oncology as measured by the number of patients in Phase IIIs, and… you can certainly see that our revenues have gone along with that." The distribution claim in BioPharmaceuticals is the only advantage management states in quantified form — about 85% of second-line-plus hypertension patients managed in primary care and specialist settings, more than 90% of cardiologists plus a majority of primary-care physicians already reached, and more than 115 countries covered by Forxiga and Lokelma [deck: ESC 2025 investor event, 31 August 2025, slide 28] — though the slide footnotes the first two figures as US-scoped internal estimates, so only the country count is externally checkable.

External sources: they corroborate the leadership claims where AstraZeneca is first and contradict them where it is not. Enhertu's standard-of-care position in HER2-positive and HER2-low breast cancer is not disputed; Tagrisso's franchise position in EGFR is attacked but not disputed. Against that, in checkpoint inhibition Keytruda recorded about $31.7bn in FY2025 at +7%, Opdivo $10.05bn at +8% and Imfinzi $6.06bn at +28% (Zacks via Yahoo Finance, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]; on a bottom-up sum of the seven disclosed checkpoint franchises Imfinzi plus Imjudo is roughly 11% of a $57bn class against Keytruda's 55% [estimate: own-filings sum of disclosed class revenue, Section 4]. Imfinzi's 28% CER growth is the best in the class off the smallest base and it comes from indications Merck under-served, so it is indication expansion into white space rather than share capture. Sanofi's own 20-F describes the mechanism that turned AstraZeneca's China revenue negative: "The recent eleventh round of VBP results remained very unfavorable to multinational companies. Domestic generic companies confirmed the existing trend, and won the main bids due to further aggressive price reductions." And GSK's Nucala won the FDA chronic obstructive pulmonary disease indication in May 2025 that AstraZeneca's Fasenra RESOLUTE trial failed to secure.

Ground-up view: innovative pharmaceuticals has two barriers on completely different time horizons. The barrier to entering the industry is very high and durable — a Phase III programme in a solid tumour costs hundreds of millions, approval requires a randomised outcome benefit, and a global launch requires a country-by-country reimbursement organisation. AstraZeneca clears it: more than 100 ongoing Phase III studies and 197 pipeline projects. That barrier explains why there are eight or ten global oncology companies rather than eighty, and it is a shared oligopoly rent, not a differentiator between AstraZeneca and Merck, Roche, Bristol Myers, Johnson & Johnson, Daiichi Sankyo, Pfizer or BeOne. The barrier to displacing an incumbent molecule, once the first is cleared, is close to zero: no installed base, no data gravity, no contract that runs, no integration cost.▪ A rival with a better randomised outcome enters the guidelines and prescribing moves. So the advantage is a set of patents with dated expiries plus a development-and-launch capability whose output has to be re-earned every year.

Daiichi Sankyo is not a supplier but a co-owner: it owns and manufactures Enhertu and Datroway, AstraZeneca books zero US Enhertu Product Sales and holds no Datroway commercialisation rights, and the flagship combination trial AVANZAR pairs Imfinzi with the partner's molecule. And buyer power is rising: managed-care and Medicare rebates grew 29% in FY2025 against 8% growth in net US Product Sales, and Calquence's US price is legislated down 41% off list from 1 January 2027, five years before its earliest US compound-patent expiry.

BioPharmaceuticals grades as two different businesses. Respiratory & Immunology holds a real barrier: the inhaled portfolio is a drug-device combination, which makes generic erosion an order of magnitude slower than for a tablet.▪ Symbicort's US Product Sales declined 9% in H1 2026, four years after Breyna became the first substitutable generic in March 2022, while Brilinta — an oral tablet one year past its generics — declined 66% CER and roxadustat 82% CER. That is roughly a seven-to-one difference in erosion rate, and it protects the sub-unit with the longest patent runway, Breztri and Trixeo at 2030–2038 in all four major markets. Cardiovascular, Renal & Metabolism has almost no advantage left: it went from +2% CER in FY2025 to −12% CER in H1 2026 and −18% CER in Q2 2026 within one quarter of Farxiga's US loss of exclusivity, its Maximum Fair Price and a lost Chinese tender bid arriving together.▪

3.2 Returns on capital

Standalone:

ROIC = NOPAT / average invested capital, where NOPAT = Reported operating profit × (1 − 20% normalised tax rate) and invested capital = total equity + net debt as the company defines it. A constant 20% rate replaces the year's effective rate because the effective rate ranges from −31.7% (FY2022) to +143.4% (FY2021) and produces meaningless results. Core ROIC substitutes Core operating profit. ROIIC = (NOPAT_t − NOPAT_t−3) / (invested capital_t − invested capital_t−3). Cost of capital for this business-quality test is taken as roughly 7–8% for a large-cap pharmaceutical company: risk-free about 4%, equity risk premium about 5%, beta 0.7–0.8, after-tax cost of debt about 3.5%, about 30% debt weight. AstraZeneca itself discloses a 7.5% post-tax weighted average cost of capital for impairment testing.

On the Reported basis AstraZeneca cleared a 7–8% cost of capital in eight of the last ten years and FY2025's 16.0% is the best of the decade; on the Core basis it has earned 18.6% to 23.3% in every year except FY2021.▪ The five-point gap is intangible amortisation on acquired and in-licensed intellectual property, and it is not obviously an add-back here: cumulative intangible amortisation plus impairment over FY2016–FY2025 was $33,460m against cumulative cash purchases of intangible assets of $15,379m plus at least $16,162m of cash paid for subsidiaries, and the cash intangible spend itself is recurring, rising and structural ($294m in FY2017 to $3,095m in FY2025).

Incremental returns match the average. Return on incremental invested capital on Core NOPAT was 19.6% over ten years, 21.0% over five and 15.2% over three — the capital deployed since 2022 (Fusion, Gracell, Amolyt, Icosavax, EsoBiotec, CinCor, FibroGen China, the Koselugo buy-in and $2,810m of FY2025 capex against $961m in FY2020) is earning below the 21% average.

Oncology's return is roughly twice the group's 15.6% Reported figure, and Rare Disease's Reported margin is about 23 points below its Core margin.▪ Purchase accounting confirms the gross margin independently: IFRS 3 required Alexion's inventory to be fair-valued at $6,769m against a pre-acquisition carrying value of $1,134m, a 6.0x uplift, which is only possible where cost of sales is a single-digit percentage of price.▪

3.4 Business-model analogues

The moat is dated molecule monopolies that a research organisation has to keep replenishing, with returns that reset at each patent expiry. The closest public comparisons are:

  • Merck & Co. The purest version of the same shape and the right primary analogue: an oncology backbone monopoly, a global trial machine and a hard exclusivity date. Both companies' returns come from patents, not customer lock-in. The analogy breaks on concentration: Keytruda was about $31.7bn in FY2025 against Imfinzi's $6.06bn, so Merck has one much better asset and one much worse cliff.
  • AbbVie. The replenishment template rather than the molecule: Humira's cliff absorbed by Skyrizi and Rinvoq is what AstraZeneca is attempting with the conjugate and bispecific wave. What carries over is the demonstration that the durable asset is the ability to develop and launch, not any one molecule. What does not carry over is the cost of doing it: AbbVie reached a 24.6% operating margin on 14.9% research intensity in FY2025 while AstraZeneca reached 23.4% on 24.2%.
  • GSK for BioPharmaceuticals specifically: same therapy areas, same inhaler device barrier, same primary-care footprint. The one difference is scale and direction: GSK's inhaled franchise is larger (Trelegy £3.0bn against Breztri's $1,199m) and already contracting, with General Medicines at −9% CER in Q2 2026, while AstraZeneca's Respiratory & Immunology still grows.
  • BioMarin for Rare Disease on shape — ultra-orphan enzyme replacement, hospital and specialist channel, six-figure annual cost, patent-plus-reformulation defence — and Vertex for the mechanism, since serial in-franchise reformulation that keeps the base and resets exclusivity is the Soliris-to-Ultomiris move. BioMarin falls short on returns (12.7% operating margin and 6.2% return on invested capital in FY2025); Vertex is in an easier competitive position, facing no approved competing mechanism in cystic fibrosis, whereas AstraZeneca's C5 franchise faces FcRn, C3, Factor B and Factor D entrants plus two eculizumab biosimilars.

Vertex earned an 86.2% gross margin and a 34.8% operating margin in FY2025. AstraZeneca does not reach those levels.▪

4. Competitive landscape and market sizing

AstraZeneca is the second-largest oncology franchise in the industry by revenue and the only one of the top five that combines top-three scale with mid-teens growth.▪ Over FY2024–FY2025 Johnson & Johnson closed from 0.93x to 0.99x of AstraZeneca's oncology revenue, so the number-two and number-three positions have converged, while AstraZeneca's gap to Merck narrowed from 1.50x to 1.40x and it passed both Bristol Myers Squibb and Roche's cancer book.▪ In BioPharmaceuticals it is second by value in SGLT-2 inhibition while disclosing that Farxiga "retained its position as the number one SGLT2 inhibitor worldwide by volume", second to GSK on respiratory scale, and the owner of the leading infant respiratory-syncytial-virus molecule while capturing only part of its in-market dollar.▪ In Rare Disease it leads complement inhibition and has been passed in the largest indication by a different mechanism.

4.1 Market structure

The market is fragmented. Built bottom-up from the fifteen largest disclosed franchises, the branded innovative oncology pool is roughly $204bn of recognised FY2025 revenue, giving a Herfindahl index of about 1,070; adding the unsized players (Astellas, Bayer, Takeda, Merck KGaA, Incyte, Exelixis, Jazz, Servier, the Chinese innovators and oncology generics) takes the pool to roughly $230–240bn and the index to about 800. By US antitrust convention that is unconcentrated. Nobody competes for "oncology". Competition happens inside mechanism-and-indication cells, and those are among the most concentrated in healthcare: the checkpoint-inhibitor class has an index above 3,600 with a single majority player and PARP inhibition has one player near 78%. Each cell inside the fragmented pool is a monopoly or duopoly with an expiry date.▪

IQVIA puts global cancer-medicine spending at $252bn in 2024 at list prices, reaching $441bn by 2029 (IQVIA Global Oncology Trends 2025, accessed 2026-08-07) [web], an implied 11.8% compound rate. That is list-price spending including generics and biosimilars, while the bottom-up $204bn is net revenue recognised by fifteen branded innovators, so net-of-rebate branded revenue below list-price spend is consistent. The share arithmetic below uses the bottom-up figure.

In the US the payer sets oncology price, through a 50.5% gross-to-net deduction and, from 2026 and 2027, through administratively set Maximum Fair Prices on Farxiga and Calquence. In Europe national payers, health-technology-assessment bodies and tender systems do, now with the EU Joint Clinical Assessment layered on — Europe Total Revenue grew 5% actual but only 1% CER in FY2025, and the 4-point difference is price. In China the state does: volume-based procurement is a reverse auction that assigns volume to the lowest bidder, so losing a bid removes the hospital channel rather than shaving price.▪

Merck states it "expects that sales of Keytruda will be materially negatively impacted by biosimilar competition between 2028 and 2029", with the primary compound patent expiring December 2028. Biosimilar pembrolizumab then puts a cheap price on the whole class. Imfinzi is the combination backbone across eleven indications, and once a cheap alternative backbone exists, every payer negotiation for an Imfinzi-containing regimen is conducted against it.▪ Both land in 2028.

The Chinese domestic PD-1 inhibitors — camrelizumab, sintilimab, toripalimab and penpulimab — are excluded from the class total above and would add roughly $3–4bn. They matter for China, AstraZeneca's second-largest market, and are not sized here.

4.3 Share counter-evidence

Ranked by how much each reshapes the structure.

  • BeOne's BRUKINSA is the largest: a rival passed AstraZeneca in a class AstraZeneca described as standard of care, and the word "Brukinsa" appears in zero of the 43 AstraZeneca earnings transcripts from 2015Q4 to 2026Q2, so AstraZeneca's own disclosure never records that the class revenue leader changed▪.
  • Chinese domestic innovators are second: Soriot conceded on the Q2 2026 call that in China "you saw the competition in the Tagrisso market. It's very, very intense. And in the ADC market, very intense too", and China was 11.3% of FY2025 Total Revenue.
  • argenx in generalised myasthenia gravis is third: a different mechanism generating about $4.2bn at +90% growth against a C5 franchise that added $445m across FY2024 and FY2025 combined, with the caveat that part of argenx's growth is in chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy and ocular disease where AstraZeneca does not compete with a C5 inhibitor.
  • Sanofi and Regeneron's Dupixent is fourth, at roughly 5x any single AstraZeneca respiratory biologic and already approved in the COPD indication AstraZeneca failed to secure.
  • Chinese and Indian generics are fifth and the most immediate: more than twenty generic bidders appeared for dapagliflozin in China's eleventh procurement round and AstraZeneca did not win a bid, and winning prices in that round were withheld from publication for the first time, so the price it would have had to match cannot be established from public sources (Caixin Global, 29 October 2025, accessed 2026-08-07) [web].

See Section 3.

5. Value chain and profit pools

AstraZeneca captures the largest profit pool in its chain, and the binding constraint is the price payers will pay.▪

The rebate dollars are not accumulating in the intermediaries' profit either. Combined operating profit of the three pharmacy benefit managers went from $18,869m (2023) to $21,565m (2025), up 14.3%, on combined revenue up 27.1%, while AstraZeneca's US contractual managed-care and Medicare rebates rose 26.5% over the same period. CVS Health Services' adjusted operating income declined in absolute dollars, from $7,312m to $7,151m. The rebate dollars pass through to plan sponsors, Part D plans and, after the Part D redesign, the government. No pharmacy benefit manager discloses rebates retained against passed through, and their segment revenue includes generics, specialty pharmacy and care delivery, so this is directional.

5.2 Bargaining power over time

AstraZeneca's share of the US list dollar over twelve years:

Year US gross $m US net $m Net as % of gross Chargebacks % Managed care and Medicare % Medicaid %
2014 23,414 10,120 43.2 11.9 33.0 5.9
2016 19,640 7,365 37.5 17.6 26.6 9.7
2018 16,538 6,876 41.6 13.4 27.8 7.9
2020 19,255 8,638 44.9 12.8 29.6 5.7
2022 32,100 17,254 53.8 7.5 27.5 5.9
2024 40,641 21,655 53.3 9.8 26.6 5.4
2025 47,385 23,444 49.5 10.8 29.5 5.3

The 2016-to-2022 improvement of 16.3 points was mix, not bargaining power: the US portfolio moved from retail primary care (Crestor, Nexium, Symbicort, heavily rebated) to hospital and specialty medicines dispensed through infusion centres and specialty pharmacy, which rebate far less.▪ Contractual rebating got worse on a like-for-like basis despite that mix shift — 29.5% of gross in 2025 against 26.6% in 2016 — so the mix masked a deterioration at the payer interface. And chargebacks, which are statutory rather than negotiated, are the fastest-growing deduction: from 7.5% of gross in 2022 to 10.8% in 2025, or $2,401m to $5,113m, against national 340B purchases growing from $66.3bn (2023) to $100.0bn (2025) (Drug Channels; Fierce Healthcare, both accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. Soriot's own view: "a number of participants are abusing this — have been abusing this 340B regulation" (Q1 2025 call).

Policy is now resetting the US price. The October 2025 agreement with the US administration provides most-favoured-nation prices to state Medicaid programmes, direct-to-consumer discounts through TrumpRx, and a three-year exemption from Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs conditional on onshoring so that substantially all medicines sold in the US are made in the US (CNBC, 10 October 2025, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. Management confirms the mechanism has already changed how it prices: "our pricing approach across all of launches now has really evolved in response to MFN. And with the U.S. now referencing a basket of countries and setting its price, we are seeing productive engagement with payers" (David Fredrickson, Q2 2026 call). Structurally that converts ex-US price negotiations from independent negotiations into inputs to the US price, so a European or Japanese payer now has leverage over the US price.▪ The size of the cut is not stated.

Medicare Part B reimburses physician-administered drugs at average sales price plus 6%, roughly plus 4.3% after sequestration, so in the buy-and-bill channel the provider's absolute margin rises with the price and the provider is not a source of price resistance the way a formulary is. From 1 January 2028 selected Part B drugs move to 106% of the Maximum Fair Price less sequestration (Avalere; Brookings, both accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. Imfinzi, Ultomiris, Soliris, Strensiq and the conjugates are all Part B buy-and-bill, and Oncology plus Rare Disease were 64% of Q2 2026 Total Revenue. Separately, Cigna's Evernorth will move to a rebate-free pharmacy benefit from 2027 for fully insured lives and 2028 as standard, delivering negotiated discounts at the point of sale instead of as post-purchase rebates (Evernorth, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. In a rebate-free world the 29.5% of gross that currently buys formulary position would have to come off list price instead, which resets Medicaid average-manufacturer-price rebates, 340B ceiling prices and every international reference price keyed to the US list.

On the marginal dollar the position is worse than the average: marginal net capture over 2022–2025 was 40.5% against a 49.5% average.

5.3 The binding constraint

Every material 2026 reversal is an exclusivity or price event: Farxiga −19% CER in Q2 2026 on US generic entry and Chinese procurement, Brilinta −63% CER, Soliris −28% CER on settled biosimilars, against Oncology +15% CER and Rare Disease +8% CER on demand. AstraZeneca also delivered its FY2025 launches on time (Section 13.4) in a year it describes as one in which "Drug shortages reached record levels… quality challenges persisted industry-wide", without a disclosed interruption.

There is no evidence of supplier power anywhere in the chain. "Most of the manufacture of APIs is delivered through the efficient use of external sourcing that is complemented by expanding use of internal capabilities" (FY2025 Annual Report), and no active-pharmaceutical-ingredient supplier and no contract manufacturer is named anywhere in the FY2025 20-F or Annual Report. Note 30 discloses total commitments of $1,727m and every dollar of it is contracted capital expenditure — there is no take-or-pay, no minimum purchase and no supplier prepayment. Trade payables are $3,820m against $10,633m of cost of sales, 131 days. The supply-chain finance programme runs through Taulia with 310 enrolled suppliers and only $100m of trade payables inside it, 2.6% of the payables book, so it is a supplier-relations tool, not leverage.

Capacity has nonetheless become a policy-imposed constraint with a deadline. The Section 232 exemption runs three years from October 2025 in exchange for onshoring, which converts a demand-driven capital plan into a compliance capital plan. Property, plant and equipment purchases went $1,361m (FY2023) to $1,924m to $2,810m (FY2025), management guides FY2026 capital expenditure up about one third on a $3.3bn base including software, and $1,420m of the $1,727m of contracted commitments falls within one year. So the constraint is two-part — revenue durability is constrained by pipeline output against the exclusivity clock, and the capital plan is constrained by a three-year policy deadline to relocate supply into the US.

The one place AstraZeneca does not control its own supply is the fastest-growing part of its revenue.▪ Daiichi Sankyo manufactures Enhertu and Datroway; Amgen manufactures Tezspire; AstraZeneca manufactures Beyfortus and sells it to Sanofi. Alliance Revenue was $3,067m in FY2025, up 38% CER, and $1,699m in H1 2026, up 29% CER against +5% CER for Product Sales. AstraZeneca discloses nothing at all about lead times, yields and quality events at Daiichi Sankyo and Amgen.

5.4 Customer-side economics and financing flows

The distributor earns roughly 1.1 cents of operating profit per list dollar and does so on negative invested capital: McKesson's cash conversion cycle is 22 days of receivables plus 24 days of inventory less 59 days of payables, or −13 days, working capital is −$9,807m, and capital expenditure plus capitalised software is 0.18% of revenue (Cencora corroborates at 0.14%). AstraZeneca has no route to squeeze a layer earning an effectively unbounded return on about 1% of the dollar, and the three national distributors moving about 78% of its US volume are not substitutable. And AstraZeneca funds the channel: its own trade receivables are $10,237m net on $55,573m of Product Sales, 67 days, while McKesson collects from pharmacies in 22 days and pays manufacturers in 59.

The 340B covered entity is a customer whose return on buying is the manufacturer's statutory discount, and that spread is AstraZeneca's chargeback line, $5,113m in FY2025, up 66% from $3,075m in 2023. No per-drug ceiling price is disclosed, so the AstraZeneca-specific spread can only be bounded from above by the chargeback line, which also includes group-purchasing, veterans' and hospital-contract chargebacks.

The gross-to-net structure is also a float: AstraZeneca invoices at gross, collects, and pays rebates later. That left a $5,941m US accrual carried forward at 31 December 2025 against $23,617m of current-year provisions, roughly 92 days, and a group accrual of $9,681m, 16.5% of Total Revenue. Any move to net pricing unwinds that float as well as the revenue, so the cash consequence of rebate reform is larger and earlier than the profit-and-loss consequence. And trade receivables measured at fair value through other comprehensive income — those the Group has the option to factor, or Chinese bank acceptance drafts — rose 4.0x to $2,681m from $667m, 26% of the $10,237m net trade receivable book. Note 17 does not split the two categories, so the China share is not established; the Board's viability stress-testing now includes a scenario of "restrictions on debt factoring".

Price is set by three pharmacy benefit managers, the US government and China's procurement authority.

6. Secular and industry trends

Oncology is the one claimed secular driver that the reported numbers show, and it is gaining share. Oncology Total Revenue went $18,447m (FY2023) to $22,352m (FY2024) to $25,619m (FY2025), a 17.8% two-year compound rate at actual FX and +14% CER in FY2025, then accelerated to +15% CER in both H1 and Q2 2026, reaching 48% of Q2 2026 Total Revenue. Against IQVIA's implied 11.8% compound rate for global cancer-medicine spending ($252bn in 2024 to $441bn by 2029, at list prices), that is roughly 3 percentage points of annual share gain, with the caveat that AstraZeneca's numerator is net of a 50.5% US deduction and IQVIA's denominator is not, so only the direction is reliable, not the level.

Growth has halved from 13.2% a year over FY2023–FY2025 to 5% CER in Q2 2026, and the flagship 2030 target is a market-growth target rather than a share-gain target. FY2023 to FY2025 Total Revenue compounded at 13.2% actual. FY2025 grew 8% CER, H1 2026 grew 6% CER and Q2 2026 grew 5% CER. Getting from FY2025's $58,739m to the $80bn 2030 ambition requires a 6.4% compound rate, and IQVIA forecasts the global medicine market at a 5–8% compound rate to roughly $2.6trn by 2030 (IQVIA, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. So the ambition implies AstraZeneca grows with its market and holds share flat for five years, at half the 13.2% rate of the last two.▪ Management does not frame it that way.

On its own cited market statistic AstraZeneca lost dollar share in FY2025, and the loss is driven by price. The FY2025 Annual Report states "Global pharmaceutical sales grew by 10.0% in 2025 (Source: IQVIA, IQVIA Midas Quantum Q3 2025)" against Total Revenue growth of 8.6% actual and 8% CER, a gap of about 1.4 points or $0.8bn. But AstraZeneca's own note says the IQVIA data are "not adjusted for Medicaid and similar rebates", while its revenue is net of the 50.5% US deduction. On the comparable invoice basis US gross Product Sales grew 16.6% against a market growing 10.0%. The correct statement is that AstraZeneca gained volume and list share and lost net-revenue share, and the gap is the rebate line.▪ The risk is price, not competitiveness, and it is no smaller: research is funded out of the net line.

Separately, AstraZeneca withdrew its per-region market-share disclosure in FY2025.▪ The FY2022, FY2023 and FY2024 reports each disclosed US, European and Japanese share and rank (US 3.4% / 12th, 3.6% / 10th, 3.5% / 12th; Europe 2.9% / 10th, 3.3% / 7th, 3.8% / 4th; Japan 4.1% / 3rd, 6.1% / 2nd, 6.5% / 2nd). The regional section retains revenue and growth and drops share and rank.

6.1 Growth attribution against three benchmarks

Organic growth. FY2020 Total Revenue $26,617m to FY2025 $58,739m, an increase of $32,122m. Deducting Alexion's FY2020 standalone revenue of about $6,100m from the base leaves an organic increase of about $26.0bn on a pro-forma base of about $32.7bn, a 12.4% compound rate [estimate: pro-forma base using Alexion's FY2020 standalone revenue]. COVID-19 medicines were a round trip inside the window and net to roughly zero at both ends — Vaxzevria $2m (2020), $3,917m (2021), $1,798m (2022) and Evusheld nil, $85m, $2,185m, then about $16m combined by FY2023 — so they do not change the five-year rate but they wreck any year-by-year comparison. Later deals added no material FY2025 revenue: Fusion, CinCor, Gracell, TeneoTwo, Amolyt, Icosavax and EsoBiotec are pre-launch or immaterial, and the FibroGen China purchase bought rights to revenue AstraZeneca was already booking. So the 12.4% organic rate over five years is real and exceptional inside its cohort, and it has ended: the realised rate is now 5–6% CER.

Against the ultimate volume driver. US Oncology Product Sales compounded at 21.4% a year from 2020 to 2025 while the CMS price index for the same franchise compounded at 1.5–2.9%, so volume — patients times days — accounts for roughly 19 of the 21.4 points. On the other side: the emerging-market off-patent brand annuity that management describes most warmly contributed −$119m to BioPharmaceuticals' FY2023–FY2025 growth.

Against industry dollars. The industry's revenue increment over FY2022–FY2025 came almost entirely from one drug class AstraZeneca does not sell. Across an 18-company large-cap cohort in dollars:

FY2022 $bn FY2025 $bn Δ $bn Compound rate
Cohort total 744.9 846.2 +101.2 4.3%
Eli Lilly + Novo Nordisk 53.6 112.0 +58.4 27.9%
Cohort excluding those two 691.3 734.2 +42.9 2.0%
AstraZeneca 44.4 58.7 +14.4 9.8%

Two companies accounted for 58% of the cohort's revenue increment and AstraZeneca for 14%, the second-largest single share and more than twice its 6% share of cohort revenue. Excluding the two, the large-cap industry grew revenue at 2.0% a year. Industry growth over the window is one drug class, and AstraZeneca's 9.8% is near the top of the rest of the cohort.

Against a peer growth cohort split by exposure. AstraZeneca ranks sixth of eighteen over three years and below the median in the latest quarter.

Cohort Members and FY22–FY25 rate Latest quarter, year on year, in dollars
Metabolic and GLP-1 Eli Lilly 31.7%, Novo Nordisk 23.2% +47.7%, +4.5%
Oncology and new-modality innovation Amgen 11.8%, Vertex 10.4%, Daiichi Sankyo 10.0%, AstraZeneca 9.8%, Novartis 9.3% +9.5%, +12.5%, +9.8%, +6.4%, +0.8%
Loss-of-exclusivity cohort GSK 5.9%, Regeneron 5.6%, Roche 3.8%, Sanofi 3.4%, Merck & Co 3.1%, Astellas 2.8%, Gilead 2.6%, AbbVie 1.8%, Bristol Myers 1.4% +5.8% to +17.5%
COVID unwind Pfizer −14.6% +2.6%

Peer median over three years, excluding Johnson & Johnson whose series is distorted by the Kenvue separation, is 5.6%, so AstraZeneca's 9.8% is 4.2 points above it and sixth of eighteen. The most recent quarter reverses the ranking: AstraZeneca's +6.4% in dollars against a peer median of +8.1%. The dollar basis flatters European and Japanese reporters translating up on a weak dollar while AstraZeneca reports in dollars and gets no translation benefit, but the direction matches AstraZeneca's own deceleration from 8% CER to 5% CER.

Franchise FY2025 CER H1 2026 CER Q2 2026 CER Market reference Implied share
Oncology +14% +15% +15% Global cancer-medicine spend at about 11.8% compound to 2029 (IQVIA, list basis) [web] gaining, about 3pp/yr
Respiratory & Immunology +12% +9% +11% Respiratory biologics and the fixed-dose triple class both growing; AstraZeneca names expanded severe-eosinophilic-asthma share for Fasenra and consistent share growth for Breztri gaining
