6.3 What changes the slope

Upward. Antibody-drug conjugates are the clearest: Enhertu Total Revenue reached $2,775m in FY2025 at +40% CER and $1,719m in H1 2026 at +32% CER, with combined AstraZeneca-plus-Daiichi-Sankyo sales of $2,961m in H1 2026 against $2,289m a year earlier, and Datroway went from $2m of Product Sales in FY2025 to $98m of Product Revenue in H1 2026. The leading indicator that this is working is Alliance Revenue, which grew 39% CER in FY2025 and 29% CER in H1 2026 against 6% for the group. Next-generation immuno-oncology bispecifics are the second, and by design they cannibalise Imfinzi. Radioconjugates, cell therapy, T-cell engagers and in vivo cell therapy are all pre-revenue. AstraZeneca's own market sizings for these — more than $80bn for conjugates, more than $10bn for radioconjugates, more than $20bn for cell therapy, more than $30bn for gene therapy — are sourced on the deck to Precedence Research and DataHorizzon at 2032, a different evidentiary standard from the IQVIA data the company uses elsewhere, and should be treated as vendor forecasts.

Downward, and dated. IQVIA expects "nearly $200 billion in brand losses through 2030 — even larger than the one the industry navigated in 2011 and 2012" [web]. AstraZeneca-specific:

Medicine FY2025 Total Revenue $m Event
Farxiga/Forxiga 8,492 US loss of exclusivity Q2 2026; UK generic Q3 2025; Japan type-2-diabetes generic Q4 2025; Chinese procurement; Maximum Fair Price effective 2026
Calquence 3,518 Maximum Fair Price effective 2027
Lynparza 3,279 US expiry 2027
Soliris 1,837 Licensed biosimilars from 1 March 2025 and November 2025
Brilinta 823 US and EU generics Q2 2025; already −66% CER in H1 2026
Total 17,949 30.6% of FY2025 Total Revenue

US net price is the second downward force. IQVIA forecasts US net-price growth of 4–7% compound through 2030 against a realised 9.4% over the past five years, with rebates and discounts now offsetting about 46% of invoice value [web]. AstraZeneca's own deduction moved 46.7% to 50.5% in a single year on the Part D redesign.

China is the third and the most abrupt. China Total Revenue was $6,654m in FY2025 at +4% CER, $3,510m in H1 2026 at −5% CER, and $1,587m in Q2 2026 at −13% CER. The mechanism is volume-based procurement, and the string "VBP" appears zero times in the FY2025 Annual Report while appearing eight times in the H1 2026 6-K. China's twelfth national procurement round in June 2026 put an estimated RMB60bn across 65 drug categories out to tender (GaBI Online; Caixin Global, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. Offsetting, the 2025 National Reimbursement Drug List added 114 drugs including 50 Class-1 innovative drugs, and China introduced its first Commercial Insurance Innovative Drug List of 19 high-cost innovative medicines effective 1 January 2026 (CMS Law; Greenberg Traurig, accessed 2026-08-07) [web] — a real new channel for patented medicines, and AstraZeneca cites both effects, with Fasenra growing 69% CER in Emerging Markets on its China listing and Enhertu 41% CER after enlistment.

Policy is the fourth, with four dated instruments: Farxiga's Maximum Fair Price effective 2026, Calquence's effective 2027, the Part D redesign effective 1 January 2025, and a three-year Section 232 tariff exemption from October 2025, conditional on onshoring, that expires around late 2028 and therefore inside the 2030 ambition window.

6.4 The exclusivity-and-launch cycle

AstraZeneca has run one full exclusivity cycle already. Total Revenue was $28,424m in 2012, declined to a trough of $22,090m in 2018 — 22% below the 2012 peak, over six years, on the Crestor, Nexium and Seroquel expiries — and did not exceed the old peak again until 2021, which took eight years plus a $39bn acquisition and a pandemic. Peak to peak, 2012 to 2025, is a 5.7% compound rate over thirteen years, close to the 5–8% market rate and close to the 6.4% the $80bn ambition implies.▪

Q2 2026 shows the legacy portfolio starting to decline and Oncology mid-upswing: Oncology +15% CER and Rare Disease +8% CER against Cardiovascular, Renal & Metabolism −18% CER, Infectious Disease −30% CER and China −13% CER, netting to +5% CER.

Of the $12,928m FY2023-to-FY2025 increase in Total Revenue, Oncology supplied $7,172m (55%), Respiratory & Immunology $2,463m (19%), Cardiovascular, Renal & Metabolism $2,253m (17%) and Rare Disease $1,362m (11%). The 17% from the cardio-renal franchise is now reversing; it was the tail of the Farxiga cycle rather than trend.▪

Management frames it differently: "we delivered strong growth in the first half, again, 11%, excluding Farxiga and Brita [Brilinta]… 6% growth overall" (Q2 2026 call). Excluding those two removes $4,184m of H1 2026 Product Revenue, 13.7% of the total. For a company whose binding constraint is replacing revenue lost to exclusivity, loss of exclusivity is the cycle, and the exclusion list renews annually. The next candidates are Lynparza in 2027 and Soliris.

6.5 What would show first if the secular story were breaking

In the order they turn: China revenue at CER, the US gross-to-net deduction rate, Oncology CER growth, Alliance Revenue as a share of Total Revenue, Tagrisso US demand, and pipeline progression events. Section 20.3 carries each one with its current reading and the level that would change the view. Two things are not in that table. Management asserted double-digit US volume and revenue growth for Tagrisso on the Q2 2026 call. And three Phase III failures have already landed on named 2030 contributors in H1 2026: CARDIO-TTRansform in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, EMERALD-2 in adjuvant hepatocellular carcinoma, and Ultomiris TMA-313.

Appendix C has the clinicaltrials.gov trial-start series by phase and the openFDA approval-event series against research spend, both pulled 7 August 2026, plus a dated list of 113 ongoing Phase III studies and their estimated primary completion dates.

7. Critical points

1. Oncology is now substituting for the rest of the company, not diversifying it. Oncology supplied 70% of group revenue growth in FY2025, 82% in H1 2026 and 109% in Q2 2026. The last of those means the non-Oncology business shrank. Group Q2 2026 Total Revenue grew $927m while Oncology grew $1,015m, against Cardiovascular, Renal & Metabolism at −18% CER and China at −13% CER. A franchise that is the only source of growth is a concentration risk rather than a diversification benefit, and its own largest medicine, Tagrisso at $7,254m, decelerated to +6% CER from +8% in H1 2026 and +10% CER in FY2025.▪

2. The loss-of-exclusivity cohort is 26% of Product Sales already running and 32% by 2027, and AstraZeneca's own erosion rates are severe. Farxiga $8,400m, Symbicort $2,885m, Soliris $1,837m, Brilinta $823m, roxadustat $274m and FluMist $272m total $14,491m, 26.1% of FY2025 Product Sales; adding Lynparza at its 2027 US expiry gives $17,770m, 32.0%.▪ Section 17.2 sets out the erosion rates the model applies, all of them AstraZeneca's own, and Section 18 the peer base rates and what has printed so far.

3. US policy is a first-order driver and it has already begun. Calquence and Farxiga already have administratively set US prices (Section 1.1). The FY2025 Annual Report mentions "Section 232" and "most favoured nation" once each and neither in the risk factors; three separate 340B actions run while AstraZeneca itself challenges 21 state statutes; and the H1 2026 6-K mentions tariffs, Section 232, most-favoured-nation pricing, TrumpRx and Maximum Fair Price zero times each across 209,941 characters. The same documents show the board treating it as first-order: "The Committee also paid particular attention to tariffs and pricing negotiations with the US Government, and the potential impact on the Group" (Audit Committee report), and the CFO's 2025 objectives included "US Tariff analysis and mitigation plans, Most Favoured Nation pricing analysis". Management's scope limitation cuts the other way: if most-favoured-nation pricing applies to new products only, then essentially the whole $21.3bn increment from FY2025 to the $80bn ambition is exposed and essentially none of the legacy base is.

4. The $80bn 2030 target is at the 96th percentile of what companies this size in this industry have achieved, and is where consensus has modelled revenues. Of 80 five-year windows in a 22-company reference class starting from a revenue base above $45bn, three cleared a +6.4% forward compound rate and all three were Pfizer: two of them the same COVID window, the third the Wyeth acquisition.▪ Even the 90th-percentile outcome at this scale is below what the ambition requires (Section 14). Conditioning on AstraZeneca's own starting growth rate does not help: of 24 windows from a $45bn-plus base with trailing growth of 5–15%, one cleared the bar. Over ten years, of 57 windows from a $45bn-plus base, the maximum realised rate was +6.3% and none cleared +6.4%. Consensus FY2030 revenue is $80,594m on 15 contributing revenue estimates, effectively the same number as the ambition, and the CFO's own datapoint at JPM in January 2026 is that consensus moved from $67bn when the target was set to about $76bn by mid-2025 to $80bn now — the street converged onto the plan rather than building to it independently.

5. The margin target requires something that has one precedent at this scale, and management no longer gives a date for it. Core operating margin was 31.7% (FY2023), 31.3% (FY2024) and 31.5% (FY2025) — unmoved for three years — against an Investor Day commitment of "mid-30s% Core operating margin by 2026".▪ The strings "mid-30s", "mid 30s", "mid-thirties" and "mid thirties" appear zero times in the FY2022, FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 Annual Reports, and zero times in the Q1 2026 and Q2 2026 earnings-call transcripts after being hedged at Q4 2025 into "while we continue to target a mid-30s operating margin in 2026, our priority remains to drive absolute profit growth". Against the base rate, a 28–36% starting operating margin has a median five-year change of −3.8 points with only 18% of windows holding or expanding, and the joint test of a +6% revenue rate with +400bp of margin expansion from a $45bn-plus base has one precedent in 80 windows, Pfizer into COVID.

6. Chinese procurement was invisible in the annual disclosure and it is the sharpest inflection in the business. "VBP", "volume-based procurement" and "NRDL" each return zero hits in the FY2025 Annual Report, published 24 February 2026, which described China as growing 4%. Five months later the H1 2026 results named volume-based procurement as one of two Total Revenue headwinds and China was −13% CER in the quarter. Farxiga's Emerging Markets revenue of $1,618m in H1 2026 at −13% CER is 2.4x its US revenue of $668m at −17%, so the geography most at risk is the one least discussed. Roxadustat, the pure China exposure, declined 82% CER in Q2 2026. What AstraZeneca does not disclose is the split of China revenue between procurement-exposed off-patent originator products and reimbursement-listed patented medicines, which determines whether −13% is a one-off reset or a multi-year decline.

7. Reported and Core are diverging as the exclusivity cycle begins, and every target is set on the higher number. Q2 2026 Reported operating profit was $3,164m against $3,508m, −10% actual and −13% CER, and Reported EPS $1.61 was −2% CER, while Core EPS rose 18% CER.▪ The gap is the widest of the twelve-quarter series; Section 13.3 takes the quarter apart and Section 14 the consensus treatment, which holds the gap flat to FY2030.

8. Capital allocation has returned 14% more cash per share over eleven years while the enterprise grew revenue 138%. Dividend per share went from $2.80 (FY2015, and flat since 2012) to $3.20 (FY2025), a 1.3% compound rate, against Core EPS compounding at 8.0%. Cumulative dividends of $43,515m exceeded cumulative free cash flow after all business development by $20,708m, a gap matched by a $20,151m increase in net debt. There have been no share repurchases in fourteen years while the share count rose (Section 12.5). AbbVie and Bristol Myers Squibb both issued stock for large deals in the same window and then repurchased $35.7bn and $31.3bn; AstraZeneca repurchased nothing. Deleveraging from 3.2x to 1.2x came from earnings growth, not repayment: gross debt declined 4% between end-2021 and end-2025 while operating profit went from $1,056m to $13,743m.

9. The Alexion acquisition returns approximately its cost of capital. AstraZeneca paid $41,058m of consideration for a business growing 22%, at a 45% premium, 6.5x last-reported revenue and 12.1x adjusted EBITDA, with 15% dilution. Under AstraZeneca ownership the same portfolio has compounded at about 6.9% adjusting for the 2023 reclassification, or 8.5% unadjusted. On a 35–50% Core operating margin applied to FY2025 Rare Disease revenue and taxed at the Core rate, the deal returns 6.7–9.6% post-tax on a $39,308m purchase enterprise value against the 7.5% post-tax weighted average cost of capital AstraZeneca itself discloses for impairment testing [estimate: franchise margin band, no segment profit exists]. $1,501m of the acquired intangibles have been fully written off (vemircopan $753m, Andexxa $504m, ALXN1840 $244m) and integration cost has reached $3,414m against an original $2.1bn estimate. The franchise earns a 43–52% Core operating margin on its own operating capital; the price paid reduces that to 6.7–9.6% post-tax.

10. The forward case is based on shipped technology; the transformative platforms are post-2030. Section 2 dates the readouts: the conjugate, bispecific, T-cell-engager, cell-therapy and radioconjugate programmes report in 2027 or later, and the CFO says many of them do not reach peak sales inside the window. Meanwhile the platform capital is already committed: $2,195m for Fusion with zero revenue, a $1.5bn Singapore conjugate plant built ahead of any wholly owned conjugate revenue, and $2bn of business-development upfronts in seven months against a stated position that no business development is needed.

8. Management claim pressure tests

Claim Source and vintage What the evidence shows Quantification
"On track to deliver ambition of $80 billion in Total Revenue in 2030" — promoted to the banner strapline of the H1 2026 results Investor Day, 21 May 2024; reaffirmed 27 July 2026 The ambition is at the 96th percentile of realised five-year growth from a $45bn-plus base and the required rate has fallen without the target changing. The bridge base moved from $45.8bn (2023) to $54.1bn (2024) and back to $45.8bn across successive decks with the endpoint fixed, so the implied rate has been 9.7%, 6.7% and now 6.4% off FY2025 actual. The financial ambitions are footnoted to Q1 2024 exchange rates in the decks only (Appendix A), so a 2030 target struck at those rates is not comparable to a reported 2030 number Requires +6.4%/yr, the 96th percentile of the reference class (Section 14). Needs $21,261m of net new revenue
"Mid-30s% Core operating margin by 2026", reaffirmed on the Q2 2024 and Q3 2024 calls and at JPM in January 2025 Investor Day CFO deck, 21 May 2024, slides 11–13 The margin has not moved in three years and the target has gone unmentioned on both 2026 calls. Reaching 34.5% in FY2026 on guidance revenue of about $62.8bn requires Core operating profit of about $21.7bn, up 17% on FY2025's $18,478m; H1 2026 Core operating profit grew 11% CER and management has guided H2 gross margin lower and H2 finance costs higher. Holding Core operating profit growth at the guided Core EPS rate gives a FY2026 Core margin of about 31.7–33.5% 1 to 3 points short [estimate: guidance-band arithmetic]. The 33.3% nine-month figure offered as proof at Q3 2025 implies a Q4 2025 Core margin of about 26.3% [estimate: 9M Core profit of $14,398m from the disclosed margin; Q4 = $4,080m on $15,503m], so the nine-month measure is not on the same seasonal base as an annual target
"We actually did achieve the goal we set ourselves 10 years ago to reach $45 billion sales in 2023… at the current exchange rates, our $45 billion goal probably is closer to $40 billion" Q4 2023 call and Investor Day 2024 FY2023 Total Revenue of $45,811m included $7,764m of Rare Disease Total Revenue, an acquired business not in the 2013 organic plan. Excluding it, FY2023 was about $38.0bn [estimate], below even the $40–42bn management itself says the target equated to at 2023 FX. The stated basis of the 2014 target was net sales; Product Sales as reported were $43,789m, 2.7% short The headline was reached; the organic path was not, and the gap was closed with the largest acquisition in the company's history. This matters directly because the $80bn ambition is explicitly stated as not contingent on future M&A
"We don't need [more business development] to deliver… this growth post 2030" Soriot, Q2 2026 call In the same period AstraZeneca paid $1,104m upfront to CSPC (with up to $3.5bn of regulatory milestones), $600m upfront plus up to $900m to Dizal explicitly to defend the Tagrisso franchise, and $200m upfront plus up to $1.9bn to CTTQ, with about $2.5bn of legacy milestones guided for FY2026 About $4.8bn a year of acquisition cash and intangible purchases in the thirty months since the "not dependent upon future M&A" slide, roughly 8% of Total Revenue (Section 11.3). H1 2026 intangible purchases alone were $3,333m against $3,095m for the whole of FY2025
"While the MFN deal presents a headwind in 2026, the effect is already factored in our guidance and can be absorbed given our large and growing revenue base" CFO, Q4 2025 call "MFN" appears exactly once in that transcript and is not quantified anywhere. On the Q2 2026 call: "we don't give brand-specific pricing commentary on MFN and don't plan to. That said, our pricing approach across all of launches now has really evolved in response to MFN", and camizestrant is named as being repriced in flight The scope limitation to new products is the exposure. The path from $58,739m to $80bn is a $21.3bn increment from at least 20 new medicines, so a scope limited to new launches exposes essentially the whole increment [estimate: arithmetic on management's own scope statement]
"Progressive dividend policy" Standing, all years The company defines progressive as "the Board intends to maintain or grow the dividend each year", which six flat years satisfied. It is a no-cut commitment, not a growth commitment Dividend per share +14% over eleven years, a 1.3% compound rate, against Core EPS +115% at 8.0%. Dividend cover on Core EPS rose from 1.5x to 2.86x, so the Board retained essentially all the earnings growth
"We really don't do a share buyback, as you know, other than to offset dilution" CFO, JPM, 13 January 2025 There were no repurchases at all in 2013–2025 and dilution was not offset (Section 12.5). On the Q3 2024 call, after a drawdown, the CFO said "we will consider and think about buybacks"; the FY2025 Annual Report filed fifteen months later repeats the 2012 suspension language verbatim Zero repurchases in fourteen years. The shares traded as low as 9,501p in 2024 and 9,667p in 2025 and stood 23% below the February 2026 high on 7 August 2026; none of those levels produced action
Calquence "is the current standard of care (SoC) across multiple forms of blood cancer" FY2025 Annual Report, Therapy Area Review BeOne reports BRUKINSA above 50% of US new-patient share in all lines of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and $382m more global and $461m more US revenue in FY2025. AstraZeneca's own language on the Q2 2026 call is narrower and consistent with that: "the leading BTK inhibitor in frontline CLL across major markets despite intense competition" Both are accurate on their own basis. AstraZeneca's depends on IQVIA revenue share for the twelve months to 30 September 2025 per its own methodology note; the rival's depends on new-patient share now, and the forward-looking one is the rival's
Imfinzi is "a leading immunotherapy approved for 11 different indications" FY2025 Annual Report On a bottom-up sum of the seven disclosed checkpoint franchises Imfinzi plus Imjudo is roughly 11% of a $57bn class against Keytruda's 55% and Opdivo's 20% [estimate: own-filings sum]. Imfinzi is the fastest-growing large asset in the class at +28% CER and the growth is indication expansion into white space rather than share capture from the leaders Keytruda about $31.7bn against Imfinzi's $6.06bn [web]. Cheap biosimilar pembrolizumab enters the same treatment lines three years before Imfinzi's own expiry (Section 4.2)
"Delivering robust and sustainable growth since acquisition of Alexion" FY2025 Annual Report, first 2025 bullet for Rare Disease The same paragraph block reports +4% actual and +4% CER growth, the slowest since acquisition and a third of FY2024's +14% CER. The C5 complement franchise that the strategy leads with — "continued leadership in complement inhibition" — was $6,110m (FY2023), $6,512m (FY2024) and $6,555m (FY2025), a 0.7% increase in FY2025, with US C5 revenue peaking in FY2024 and European C5 declining for two consecutive years The franchise was 81.2% weighted to C5 at the FY2022 base and C5 delivered 40% of the three-year growth, a 0.49x contribution ratio. Strensiq was 13.6% of the base and delivered 35% (2.6x); Koselugo 2.9% and 22% (7.6x). Rare Disease did re-accelerate to +11% CER in H1 2026, so FY2025's 4% is not the current run-rate
Rare Disease patient growth demonstrates the franchise's momentum Investor Day 2024, slides 79, 82, 83 The only place AstraZeneca published a volume series beside revenue, and it shows realised price falling. Patient growth of +18%, +21% and +25% (FY2022, FY2023, Q1 2024) against Total Revenue growth of +10%, +12% and +16% at CER implies revenue per patient declining about 7% a year; in neurology, the fastest-growing part, patient growth of +15%, +40% and +42% against revenue growth of +11%, +15% and +23% implies about −4%, −18% and −13%. Management explained the gap itself at the same event as product mix plus geographic mix The franchise converts roughly 55–65% of its volume growth into revenue growth. AstraZeneca stopped disclosing the patient series after Q1 2024, so it cannot be tested from the filings whether the gap has narrowed
The Soliris-to-Ultomiris conversion demonstrates "proven impressive product conversion expertise" Investor Day 2024 It is a deliberate price cut bought with a decade of exclusivity, and three independent methods agree on the size. US list price times label dosing puts Ultomiris about 10% below Soliris in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and aplastic haemolytic uraemic syndrome and 26–33% below in neurology; Canada's CADTH comparison for neuromyelitis optica gives −25.0%; Alexion's own CEO said "the price of Ultomiris is about 30% lower than that of Soliris" On about $6.6bn of C5 revenue, converting a neurology patient trades roughly 28% of revenue per patient for extending exclusivity from 2027 to 2035. Rational, and it means the C5 franchise cannot grow revenue at its patient-growth rate while conversion continues
Ultomiris indication expansion is worth "$5bn+ Peak Year Revenue, non-risk adjusted" across five indications and more than 700k diagnosed patients Investor Day 2024, slide 86 Two years later: ARTEMIS in cardiac-surgery-associated acute kidney injury was discontinued in April 2026 "due to lack of efficacy following a planned interim analysis"; the adult haematopoietic-stem-cell-transplant trial missed event-free survival; ICAN in IgA nephropathy met its endpoint and is filed into a market already holding Filspari, Tarpeyo, Fabhalta and Vanrafia; lupus nephritis and delayed graft function are unread One of five read out positive, into the one indication of the five whose 400,000-patient population makes it a competitive nephrology market rather than an ultra-orphan monopoly. The C5 franchise grew 0.7% in FY2025 and 5.0% in H1 2026
"Brand recovery in the midterm, and we saw the similar trend with the Betaloc and CRESTOR in the past" for Farxiga in China Iskra Reic, Q4 2025 call The analogy is not quantified anywhere by the company, and the global version of the same annuity did not appear in the numbers: Crestor, Seloken and Pulmicort subtracted from BioPharmaceuticals' FY2023–FY2025 growth (Section 6.1). The China-specific version would have to be tested against Crestor's and Betaloc's China lines around their 2019–2020 procurement rounds, which appear in the FY2019–FY2022 annual reports If the analogue fails, the cardio-renal decline is a step-down rather than a trough
"Our four guiding principles — Access, Value, Sustainability and Equity" opens the pricing risk factor FY2025 20-F Item 3.D The pricing risk factor became less specific as pricing got worse. FY2021 listed seven named mechanisms including payer consolidation, price transparency and reference pricing; by FY2024 all three had been deleted. FY2025's version opens with three paragraphs of philosophy before naming any mechanism, and names only the EU Joint Clinical Assessment, the Inflation Reduction Act and unnamed "health equalisation initiatives" Over the same window the US gross-to-net deduction reached 50.5%, two medicines received administered prices, and China went from +4% to −13% CER
Fixed-duration treatment is a Calquence growth driver — "supported by the clear global trend towards adoption of finite duration treatments" Q2 2026 call A 14-cycle fixed regimen displaces treat-to-progression dosing, which in front-line chronic lymphocytic leukaemia runs for years, so each converted patient raises the patient count and lowers lifetime revenue per patient. The mechanism is already visible in independent data Imfinzi's Medicare Part B units per beneficiary declined from 744 to 715, −1.0% a year, between 2020 and 2024 as the mix shifted toward fixed perioperative courses, while its beneficiary count grew 12.7% a year
More than 90% of small-molecule discovery is AI-enabled, "potentially improving the probability of clinical success" FY2025 Annual Report, CEO Review Every disclosed AI metric is an input: share of pipeline AI-enabled, employees trained, X-rays processed, sites deployed. The two innovation key performance indicators count events rather than success rates, so the internal scorecard would not reveal an improvement in probability of success if there were one. Independent analysis finds AI-discovered molecules failing Phase II at historic rates and no AI-discovered drug approved Quantitative Continuous Scoring is the exception and has a dated prospective test in AVANZAR in H2 2026: response rate 36.8% against 15.3% for docetaxel in biomarker-positive non-squamous patients, progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.57, with the cut point optimised retrospectively
"The aggregate probability of success that we use across our pipeline… it's around 60%… we have consistently developed higher… 75% plus has been our record" Soriot, Q2 2026 call The industry benchmark is consistent with the published dataset (Phase III to filing 57.8%, filing to approval 90.6%, so 52.4% for the chain). The 75%-plus claim has no disclosed denominator, period or definition, so it cannot be audited from the filings. The realised record in the most recent reported half was four of seven Phase III readouts meeting their primary endpoint, 57% on a small sample Recent counter-evidence is dense: LATIFY, SAMETA, RESOLUTE, PROSPERO and CARDIO-TTRansform all missed in four quarterly announcements, plus ARTEMIS discontinued and the adult HSCT-TMA trial missed
Company guidance is beatable, given a 95% hit-or-beat rate over ten years and no full-year cut in eleven Guidance record, FY2016–FY2026 The upward revisions stopped. FY2025 was the first year since FY2020 with no upward revision at any quarter, and it landed at the centre of the revenue band and the bottom third of the EPS band. Q4 2025 standalone was +4% actual and +2% CER on revenue with Core EPS +1% actual and −2% CER. FY2026 is being reconfirmed rather than raised, with H1 at +6% CER and Q2 at +5% CER against a band of roughly 5–9% Reconfirming mid-to-high single digit after Q2 at +5% CER requires H2 at roughly +6% to +12% CER, flat to accelerating, while the Farxiga loss of exclusivity moves from a partial-period to a full-period drag. Management gave no H2 phasing
Q2 2026's +18% CER Core EPS growth demonstrates upside to the low-double-digit full-year guide Q2 2026 results The CFO attributes part of it to a one-off: the Q2 tax rate "benefited from a onetime adjustment to deferred tax assets following certain internal legal entity changes". Reported EPS in the same quarter was $1.61, −2% at CER Q2 revenue growth was +5% CER. Part of the +18% is the deferred-tax adjustment, not operating leverage

Five inflections:

  • 2014–2016: independence defended, and paid for out of the balance sheet. The board rejected £55.00 per share and defended the rejection with a public revenue commitment. Revenue then declined from $24,708m (FY2015) to $22,090m (FY2018). Three financing consequences are computable: externalisation income stood in for missing profit (FY2016 Externalisation Revenue $1,683m, 7.3% of Total Revenue, while Core operating profit was $6,721m); the dividend was not covered by operating cash flow less capital expenditure for five consecutive years, by a cumulative $7,130m; and total equity declined from $19,646m (FY2014) to $12,468m (FY2018), 36%, while long-term debt rose from $14,137m to $17,359m. The priority order has not changed since: research is protected first (never below $5,757m through the trough, with intensity rising to 26.9% in FY2018 as revenue declined), then the dividend, then the balance sheet.
  • 27 July 2017: one announcement carried MYSTIC's failure plus PACIFIC and FLAURA. Management kept Imfinzi but moved its centre of gravity from first-line combination to earlier-stage consolidation, and moved Tagrisso into first line. Soriot on the call: PACIFIC's indication "is still underestimated. It has a lot of potential, and we will be by ourselves in that indication." Oncology went from 16% of Product Sales in FY2016 to 43.6% of FY2025 Total Revenue and 48% of Q2 2026. The same response came nine years later on CARDIO-TTRansform: the ambition "assumes successes and setbacks".
  • December 2020 to July 2021: Alexion, and the switch from asset sales to acquired revenue. The deal did what the CFO said it would at announcement — it bought the cash-flow cover that unlocked a dividend frozen since 2014, with operating cash flow going $4,799m (FY2020) to $14,575m (FY2025) and free cash flow covering the dividend 2.4x by FY2025. It also bought the slowest of the three franchises: Rare Disease grew 4% actual in FY2025 against Oncology's 15%, and re-accelerated to 11% CER in H1 2026, still well below the 24% growth rate quoted at announcement.
  • FY2022–FY2025: the cash turn is large and the margin turn is small. Revenue 2.21x from FY2020 to FY2025, operating cash flow 3.04x, and cash after capital expenditure and dividends from $266m to $6,794m. But Core operating margin moved 3.9 points over five years and only 2.3 points over ten (29.2% in FY2016 to 31.5% in FY2025) on 2.55x revenue. The numeric margin target exists only in event transcripts and decks, never in the audited disclosure, and FY2026 guidance covers revenue, Core EPS growth and the Core tax rate with no margin line.
  • 2026: the first real loss-of-exclusivity year, Chinese procurement and a Phase III failure inside eight weeks. Revenue held: an $8,400m medicine, 14.3% of FY2025 Total Revenue, lost US exclusivity, China declined 13% CER, and Total Revenue still grew 5% CER. Reported operating profit did not: it declined 10% actual and 13% CER, and EPS declined 2% CER while Core EPS rose 18% CER. The Core-to-Reported gap is widening.

Behaviours visible more than once in the record:

  • Research is never the adjustment variable. Intensity rose to 26.9% in the FY2018 trough, and Reported research rose 13% CER in H1 2026 with two products rolling off and a Phase III failure booked.
  • The dividend is defended past cash coverage and the buyback is not a tool, at 1.3x net debt to EBITDA and after fourteen years.
  • Equity is issued when the pipeline needs funding, and it dilutes.
  • Asset sales substitute for growth when growth is absent and stop when it returns, so it is dormant.
  • A failed trial produces redirection rather than retreat.
  • Numeric financial targets live in investor events while the Annual Report contains only revenue and medicine counts, so a target's presence in the audited disclosure is a reliable signal of how firmly it is held.

Episodes the current account omits. Externalisation is gone from the current disclosure: "Externalisation is a core component of our strategy" (FY2016) has no counterpart caption today, and the current filings do not show that 7.3% of FY2016 revenue came from that line. COVID-19 is absent from a growth story it once supported, and the company does not claim it as a resilience result. And the mid-30s margin commitment appears in no Annual Report from FY2022 to FY2025.

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

10.1 Who runs the company

Role Person First appointed Tenure at 7 Aug 2026 Prior record
CEO, Executive Director Pascal Soriot 1 October 2012 13.8 years COO of Roche Pharmaceuticals; before that CEO of Genentech. External hire, knighted 2022
CFO, Executive Director Aradhana Sarin 1 August 2021 5.0 years CFO of Alexion, arriving with the acquisition; before that Citi, UBS, JP Morgan. Medical doctor by training
Non-Executive Chair Michel Demaré Board September 2019, Chair April 2023 6.9 years on the Board Judged independent on appointment as Chair

Soriot is one of the longest-serving CEOs in large-cap pharmaceuticals, and CEO succession disclosure in a fourteenth year is thin. The Nomination and Governance Committee describes its work as having "included desktop research relating to potential external candidates and continued monitoring of the development of potential internal candidates". The Board began receiving "regular updates on Executive Director succession planning" in response to the 2024 board evaluation, which implies it was not receiving them regularly before, and "Board and executive succession planning" is listed as a 2026 priority.

Executive turnover has been low with two consequential exits. Mene Pangalos, EVP BioPharmaceuticals research and a Senior Executive Team member from 2013, retired in early 2024. Leon Wang, EVP International and China President, was placed on extended leave in late 2024 while under investigation and replaced by Iskra Reic in December 2024. In November 2025 the Shenzhen Prosecutor indicted AstraZeneca Investment (China) Co., Ltd., the former EVP and one former senior employee on charges of unlawful collection of personal information and illegal trade, with the two individuals additionally indicted on charges of medical insurance fraud. The cases are consolidated before the Shenzhen City Intermediate Court with no trial date scheduled. AstraZeneca prepaid RMB 24m (about $3.5m) of unpaid import taxes in October 2025 relating to Imfinzi, Imjudo and Enhertu as voluntary compensation, and a fine of one to five times that amount may still be levied. Against that, more than 70% of changes within the executive cohort in 2025 were internal appointments.

Marcus Wallenberg is the only Non-Executive Director the Board does not consider independent — a director of Astra since May 1989 and of AstraZeneca since 1999, and a Non-Executive Director of Investor AB, which holds 3.33% of the share capital — and he attended 6 of 12 Science Committee meetings and 3 of 5 Sustainability Committee meetings across 2024–2025. Those two committees validate the stretch and the outcome of 30% of the annual bonus and 40% of the long-term plan.

Base-pay increases are capped at the UK all-employee budget and the pension allowance matches the wider workforce. The leverage is entirely in the variable multiples. Weighting each metric by the CEO's maximum opportunity:

Metric Share of maximum variable pay
Science and innovation event and volume counts 30.0%
Total Revenue (absolute, gross, at budget FX) 22.6%
Cash flow (operating cash less capital expenditure, adding back intangible-disposal proceeds) 20.0%

  • 42.6% of maximum variable pay is tied to two absolute size-based measures that an acquisition increases with no charge for the capital used. Total Revenue is gross revenue including Alliance and Collaboration Revenue, and the cash-flow metric is defined as operating cash flow less capital expenditure adding back intangible-disposal proceeds, so cash spent acquiring a business is not deducted and neither is the equity issued to pay for it. Alexion cost $41bn in cash and stock and added $9,126m of FY2025 Total Revenue plus its operating cash flow; every dollar flows positively through both metrics and the purchase price appears in neither.
  • Only 5.2% is tied to a per-share measure, and that measure is Core EPS, which excludes the intangible amortisation where the cost of acquired molecules appears: FY2025 Reported EPS was $6.60 against Core EPS of $9.16, and no metric anywhere in the plan is set on the lower number.
  • The share count is not in the plan, and it rose over the decade to FY2025 (Section 12.5).
  • The one financial target management repeatedly gave the market is absent from the plan. There is no margin metric in either the bonus or the long-term plan, so no part of executive pay depends on closing the gap from 31.5% to mid-30s.
  • No bonus target is disclosed prospectively. All five 2026 bonus metrics are marked commercially sensitive, as were the 2025 metrics in the prior report, and the long-term plan's Total Revenue hurdle is withheld on the same grounds, so roughly 30% of the bonus and 20% of the long-term award run against hurdles no outside shareholder can see, in a currency basis the company says is "not directly comparable year-on-year".

The long-term plan vested at an average 90.5% of maximum over ten years and never below 79%; cumulative CEO realised pay 2016–2025 is £149,500,000. The 2023 award vested at 97%. Its Total Revenue threshold for 20% vesting was $43bn against FY2022 actual Total Revenue of $44,351m, so the floor paid out even on a 3.0% three-year decline, and full vesting required $50.5bn, a 4.4% compound rate. The outcome was $59.0bn at budget rates, overshooting the maximum by 16.8%. Four of the six metrics paid in full and only relative total shareholder return — the sole externally benchmarked metric — paid less than maximum, at 17% of its 20% weight on a sixth-of-nineteen ranking. The 2026 grant lowered the new-molecular-entity volume hurdle by 21.4% at both threshold and maximum.

The Committee discloses the gap it intends to close — CEO target total direct compensation of £11.74m against a global-pharmaceutical median of £13.9m, an 18.4% shortfall — states "we aspire to close this gap over time", benchmarks against a group of eight US companies (AbbVie, Amgen, Bristol Myers Squibb, Eli Lilly, Gilead, Johnson & Johnson, Merck & Co, Pfizer) rather than the seven European peers it also discloses, and states "Our Policy will be due for renewal at the 2027 AGM". It states separately that there are no pay changes arising from the US listing harmonisation itself.

The CEO's beneficial shareholding declined 12.7% during 2025, from 269,861 to 235,607 Ordinary Shares, in a year in which 121,091 shares were released to him (110,412 from deferred-bonus and performance-share awards plus 10,679 dividend-equivalent shares) at a three-month average price of 13202p. The annual disclosure does not reconcile the two movements, and the minimum-shareholding-requirement table shows the 235,607 decomposing into beneficial and unvested components, so part of the change is presentation rather than sale. The CFO's holding rose 20.5% over the same year, from 117,364 to 141,395 shares.

Business development gross was $46,700m over the eleven years — acquisitions of subsidiaries $18,797m, purchases of intangible assets $16,839m, contingent consideration paid $7,599m, the Acerta share-purchase liability $2,620m, acquisition-related employee share awards $513m and non-controlling-interest purchases $332m — which is 63% of operating cash flow and 3x property capital expenditure. The eleven years split into two eras. FY2021–FY2025: operating cash flow $52,552m, business development 56% of it, dividends 42%.

Cumulative dividends of $43,515m exceeded cumulative free cash flow after all business development by $20,708m; net debt rose $20,151m, from $3,223m at 1 January 2015 to $23,374m at 31 December 2025. Cash after investment did not fund both the dividend and the deals.

Revenue grew 138% and 94% per share; Core operating profit 168% and 118%. Capital productivity was essentially flat across the decade: Core operating profit over invested capital was 26.3% (FY2015), 26.5% (FY2020), 15.6% (FY2021 on the Alexion goodwill) and 25.6% (FY2025). Incremental pre-tax return on the $45,822m of invested capital added over the decade was 25.3%, or 20.2% at a 20% tax rate, which is close to but not above what the FY2015 business already earned.

Goodwill plus other intangibles was $59,088m at 31 December 2025, 52% of total assets and 121% of shareholders' equity. Goodwill impairment has been nil in every year from FY2017 to FY2025. That is not evidence the acquisitions worked: Note 10 tests goodwill at the operating-segment level and there is one operating segment, with recoverable amount "determined on a fair value less costs to sell basis using the market value of the Company's outstanding Ordinary Shares", so the test cannot fail while market capitalisation exceeds book equity, which it does by a wide margin. Disappointment surfaces at the product-intangible level instead, where the cash-generating unit is the individual product: gross intangible impairment charges were about $6.8bn across 2018–2025 ($709m, about $1,034m, $405m, $2,067m, $318m, $434m, $1,577m, $218m), virtually all of it acquired intellectual property, against zero goodwill impairment on $21,242m of goodwill.

10.5 Capital allocation: stated framework against revealed behaviour

The stated priorities, unchanged in wording since FY2021: "investing in the business and pipeline; maintaining a strong, investment-grade credit rating; potential value-enhancing business development opportunities; and supporting the progressive dividend policy." Share repurchase is not in the list. The 2014 deck quantifies what was given up, with $53bn returned to shareholders over 2004–2013 of which $27.8bn was dividends and $25.4bn buybacks, peaking at $6.0bn in 2011 [deck: Investor Day 2014, slide 7].

Stated Revealed FY2015–FY2025 Match
Invest in the business and pipeline first Research $93,874m expensed (24.5% of revenue); business development cash $46,700m (63% of operating cash flow); property capex $15,360m (21%) Yes, and the ordering is real — business development outspent capex 3:1
Maintain a strong investment-grade rating Net debt $3,223m to $23,374m; leverage peaked at 3.2x in FY2021 and is 1.2x at FY2025; ratings retained and upgraded through the acquisition Yes on outcome; the FY2021 peak shows the constraint is soft rather than binding
Value-enhancing business development 25.3% pre-tax incremental return on invested capital; no goodwill impairment; no disclosed hurdle rate, target return or post-completion review Not verifiable at the aggregate level
Support the progressive dividend policy Dividend per share +14% over eleven years, six of them flat; dividends exceeded free cash flow after business development by $20,708m against a $20,151m rise in net debt Yes to the letter of "maintain or grow"; no to any reading of it as growth
Buybacks "to offset dilution" (CFO, JPM January 2025) Zero repurchases 2013–2025; the share count rose No

The framework is silent on the numbers: there is no disclosed hurdle rate, no target return on invested capital, no target payout ratio, no target leverage range beyond "strong, investment-grade", and no stated condition under which the 2012 suspension would be lifted. The Board's own account of approving 2026 capital expenditure lists only qualitative considerations: "alignment of the capital spend to strategic priorities, business needs and delivery of Ambition 2030". No financial return criterion is stated.

The $50bn covers "manufacturing and R&D" through 2030 with no disclosed split. Extrapolating FY2025 group research of $14,232m and capital expenditure of $2,810m at revenue growth, and allocating the US 40–50% of both (the US was 42% of FY2025 revenue, projected by management to reach about 50% by 2030), gives $43–61bn of on-trend US manufacturing-and-research spend over 2026–2030 [estimate: FY2025 lines extrapolated at revenue growth, US share proxied by revenue share]. The $50bn figure is inside that band, so it may contain little or no increment. The conditionality is new: the spend is now a condition of a three-year tariff exemption.

The current state is worse than FY2025 suggests. H1 2026 operating cash flow declined 12% to $6,224m while property capital expenditure rose 20% and intangible purchases rose 85% to $3,333m (including the $1,104m CSPC upfront). Free cash flow after capital expenditure and intangibles was $1,581m against $4,207m a year earlier, a 62% decline, against $3,288m of dividends paid in the half. Net debt rose $3,538m in six months to $26,912m, including $2,407m of commercial paper that was nil at year end. The 2026 outflow commitments already disclosed — about $4.4bn of capital expenditure, about $2.5bn of milestone payments and about $5.1bn of dividends — total roughly $12bn against FY2025 operating cash flow of $14,575m, before any new business development. It is the eleven-year pattern: when investment demand rises, the dividend is held and net debt absorbs the difference.

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

AstraZeneca is an in-licensor and bolt-on acquirer that overpaid once at scale, and its two best deals were struck a decade ago. The two transactions that rebuilt the company were bought cheaply: the February 2014 buyout of Bristol Myers Squibb's half of the diabetes alliance brought dapagliflozin, which reached $8,400m of Product Sales in FY2025 against a recognised acquisition cost of roughly $8.4bn including the day-one fair value of the contingent royalties, and the February 2016 majority investment in Acerta Pharma brought acalabrutinib, which reached $3,518m against about $6.4bn of total cash paid across nine years. Neither intangible has ever been impaired. The largest deal has landed at roughly its cost of capital. The 2012–2013 biotech bolt-ons were close to a total loss, with named write-offs of $2,175m across three deals. And for six years a third of Reported operating profit came from selling medicines rather than operating them.

Goodwill of $21,242m has never been impaired and two acquired molecules built two of the three franchises. But no deal since 2016 has been bought at the prices paid for Farxiga and Calquence, the one large deal since is a cost-of-capital outcome, and the profit that flattered the 2015–2020 accounts came from divesting the back catalogue.

11.2 Synergies, round trips and terms changed under pressure

The Alexion synergy target of about $500m a year pre-tax was confirmed once, on the Q3 2021 call, and after 2022 was never reported against separately — it was folded into a post-acquisition group review, which discloses a run-rate benefit, not a synergy. The integration programme itself was revised twice: announced at about $2.1bn of one-time cost for about $1.2bn of run-rate benefit by end-2025, revised in FY2022 to about $2.9bn plus about $0.9bn of capital expenditure, with charges taken of $1,030m, $675m, $362m, $1,115m and $232m across 2021–2025, or $3,414m against the original $2.1bn estimate. The benefit target was raised to about $2.2bn by end-2026 with $1.5bn stated as realised at 31 December 2024, and completion slipped from end-2025 to end-2026, and to end-2030 for the enterprise-resource-planning project.

Koselugo is the first of three round trips: half the global economics were sold to MSD in July 2017 as part of a deal worth up to $8.5bn to AstraZeneca, and bought back in August 2025 for $150m upfront plus up to $810m. Synagis and Beyfortus: US Synagis rights were sold to Sobi for a $515m gain plus a participation right in future US nirsevimab profits, for which $400m was received in three tranches; in 2023 the participation was replaced by a royalty and AstraZeneca recorded a $712m gain on extinguishing the liability. The end state is that AstraZeneca books $703m of Beyfortus Total Revenue of which only $281m is Product Sales, and the US "Product Sales" of $184m are manufactured product sold to Sanofi. In June 2026 AstraZeneca commenced arbitration against Sanofi before the International Chamber of Commerce over alleged non-performance under the Beyfortus collaboration; Sanofi has filed counterclaims, and the matter appears nowhere in the FY2025 20-F. US Toprol-XL to Aralez in 2016 for $175m plus milestones and royalties ended in Aralez's bankruptcy and a $14m provision, and the royalty stream was lost.

Definiens and Syntimmune both went to litigation. Definiens is unresolved twelve years on. Syntimmune: a Delaware court held in September 2024 that a $130m milestone had been achieved and that AstraZeneca had breached its contractual obligation to use commercially reasonable efforts, and in June 2025 awarded a further $181m in damages, for $311m of adverse determinations to date, with AstraZeneca's counterclaim continuing.

And the largest M&A decision in the record was a refusal. Pfizer's final proposal of £55.00 per share was rejected on 19 May 2014 as inadequate; the London line closed at 11,896p on 7 August 2026, 2.2x the rejected price before dividends and roughly 2.6x including the dividends declared across 2014–2025 [estimate: summing disclosed annual dividends per Ordinary Share].

11.3 Business development is running at about 8% of revenue, against a stated position that it is not needed

Since the May 2024 slide stating the $80bn ambition is "not dependent upon future M&A", AstraZeneca has committed $2,771m of acquisition cash and $2,662m of intangible purchases (2024), $66m and $3,095m (2025), and $3,333m of intangible purchases in H1 2026 alone — $11,927m in thirty months, about $4.8bn a year. On an annualised basis H1 2026 licensing spend runs at about $6.7bn, more than the entire 2015–2020 six-year total of $6,076m. The company also flipped from a net seller of product rights to a heavy net buyer: intangible purchases less disposals were a net $3,222m inflow in 2015–2020 and a net $9,179m outflow in 2021–2025, with a further $3,168m of net outflow in H1 2026. Note 30 discloses $10,182m of potential development milestones ($1,226m within one year) and $21,301m of potential revenue milestones, all maximum contractual amounts, undiscounted, not risk-adjusted, with a general right to terminate at no cost.

12. Capitalisation and balance sheet

At 30 June 2026 AstraZeneca held $32,239m of gross debt against $4,893m of cash, for net debt of $26,912m, up $3,538m in six months. Trailing-twelve-month EBITDA is $20,326m, so leverage is 1.32x net and 1.59x gross, against 1.20x and 1.52x at 31 December 2025. The debt is entirely unsecured, has no financial covenants anywhere in bonds or facilities, and is rated A1 / A+, three notches above where S&P had the company in 2020.

12.2 Maturity wall and refinancing cost

Contractual obligations, undiscounted: $5,966m within one year, $8,814m in one to three years, $7,629m in three to five years, $17,338m beyond five, of which $8,223m is contractual interest.

Applying AstraZeneca's own 7 August 2026 secondary curve (2027 4.19%, 2030 4.70%, 2031 4.75%, 2034 5.09%, 2037 5.38%, 2051 5.77%) to the pro-forma stack, refinancing the entire $26.6bn at today's rates costs +$254m a year, 19% of the FY2025 interest line and 1.3% of FY2025 EBITDA. The 6.45% 2037 bond is a $29m annual saving when it refinances, offsetting a ninth of the total. The concentrated exposure is a single tranche: $4,415m of sub-2.5%-coupon bonds maturing 2028–2030 at a 1.24% weighted coupon refinancing at about 4.50%, for +$144m a year, 0.7% of EBITDA, or about +$48m a year spread over three years. The 2027 wall is cost-neutral at a 4.00% coupon against a 4.19% market yield. Refinancing capacity: $5,733m outstanding under a Euro Medium Term Note programme, $21,369m under an SEC-registered programme, $4,875m of undrawn committed facilities to April 2031, and $2bn placed in February 2026.

12.3 Covenants, security and structural seniority

There are no financial covenants anywhere: Note 28 states the committed bank facilities have none, the going-concern note repeats it, and nothing in the bond documentation is disclosed as covenanted. This removes the entire covenant-proximity category of balance-sheet risk. The only security AstraZeneca has granted is to its own pension trustee rather than a lender: a charge over the Cambridge Biomedical Campus in favour of the UK Pension Fund Trustee, valued at £317m and capped at £350m, exercisable only in a Group insolvency event.

Structural subordination is explicit and material. The USD notes are issued by AstraZeneca Finance LLC and guaranteed by AstraZeneca PLC, and the 6-K states they are "structurally subordinated to indebtedness and other liabilities of the subsidiaries of AstraZeneca PLC, none of which guarantee the AstraZeneca Finance USD Notes." At 30 June 2026 the combined obligor group held $128m of assets against $29,436m of liabilities, with $25,273m due from non-guarantor subsidiaries, zero revenue and a $523m loss for the half. That does not change default probability at A1/A+ and it does change recovery. The same structure constrains the dividend: distributable reserves were $14,461m at 31 December 2025, dependent on subsidiaries settling intercompany receivables "within a reasonable period of time", against an intended FY2026 dividend of about $5.1bn, 2.8 years of cover on the stock of reserves.

12.4 Leases, pension and liquidity

Lease liabilities grew from $675m in FY2019 to $1,803m in FY2025 and $2,748m at 30 June 2026, a 52% increase in six months on the US property lease, with $354m of signed-but-not-commenced leases still to arrive. Right-of-use assets were $1,741m net.

The pension is a $999m deficit on a $7,480m obligation across more than 50 plans in 28 countries, with the UK 64% of obligations and Sweden 22%. It is not a structural risk because the hedging is close to complete: the UK interest-rate hedge is 100% of assets against a 100% target, the inflation hedge 96%, a 2013 longevity swap covers about 7,500 pensioners and roughly $2.0bn of liability, and 87% of unintended non-sterling currency risk in UK assets is hedged. The largest single sensitivity is $367m from a 50bp fall in the discount rate, mostly offset by the asset hedge. Scheduled cash is small: about $81m of FY2026 contributions plus £39m annual UK deficit payments to March 2028. The ten-year deficit path peaked at $(3,202)m in FY2020.

AstraZeneca went from zero short-dated wholesale funding to $2.4bn in one quarter and the resources-to-one-year-borrowings ratio compressed from 3.0x to 1.6x, the lowest in the ten-year record. That is not distress at A1/A+ with $4.9bn of covenant-free facility headroom, but a forward model should start from this funding mix. The size of the commercial paper programme is not disclosed anywhere in the 20-F, the Annual Report or the 2026 interims. The facility itself was cut by $2,000m in 2024, from $6,875m to $4,875m, and has not been restored.

The deleveraging from 3.21x to 1.20x was earnings-driven rather than repayment-driven: gross debt at 31 December 2025 was $1,159m below the FY2021 peak, a 3.8% reduction, while EBITDA grew 157%. The ratio depends on earnings: at FY2023 EBITDA of $13,580m, today's $26,912m of net debt would be 1.98x.

Ratings went the other way through the largest acquisition in the company's history. S&P had AstraZeneca at BBB+ from 2017 to 2020, on BBB+ CreditWatch Positive at end-2020, A− by end-2021, A in 2022 and A+ by 2024; Moody's held A3 with a negative outlook through 2021, never downgraded, and moved to A2 in 2023 and A1 in 2025. Alexion was mostly equity-funded, which is why the ratings improved. The short-term upgrade to P-1 / A-1 in 2023, from P-2 / A-2 held from at least 2016, is what makes the 2026 commercial paper draw possible; a two-notch long-term move would plausibly close that window.

The one episode of real balance-sheet strain was 2017–2019, not the Alexion year: net debt rose from $10,657m to $13,003m while EBITDA declined, taking leverage to 1.82x and net debt to 48.1% of net debt plus equity, the highest of the decade; the dividend consumed 99%, 135% and 121% of operating cash flow in FY2017, FY2018 and FY2019; S&P downgraded and Moody's ran a negative outlook. The gap was closed with product divestments booked in Other operating income, the April 2019 equity placing and capital expenditure held below $1bn. That is the relevant precedent if the current investment programme outruns cash flow.

Currencies and fiscal-year ends differ, so only leverage compares, and even it mixes as-of dates. AstraZeneca is just below the median on leverage (1.32x against a peer median of 1.59x), at the low end on debt-to-equity (60.8% against a median near 88%), and in the upper half on rating — behind Johnson & Johnson, Roche, Novo Nordisk, Novartis, Eli Lilly, Sanofi and Merck & Co on Moody's, and level with Merck on S&P.

12.7 Structural balance-sheet risks

  1. Investment spending, not refinancing, is what could re-lever this balance sheet. FY2026 capital expenditure is guided up about a third on $3,270m against a $50bn announced US programme; contracted capital expenditure not yet provided for is $1,727m with $1,420m within one year; the CSPC upfront alone was $1.2bn with up to $3.5bn behind it; and Note 30 discloses $10,182m of potential development milestones. Against $14,575m of FY2025 operating cash flow and about $5.1bn of dividends, roughly $6bn a year is free for all of it before business development.
  2. Commercial paper reliance depends on a three-year-old short-term rating, and the programme size is undisclosed. $2,407m outstanding, up from zero, on a P-1 / A-1 that dates only from 2023.
  3. The step-up on the 2028–2030 low-coupon tranche: $4,415m at 1.24% refinancing near 4.50% for +$144m a year, 0.7% of EBITDA.
  4. Structural subordination of the guaranteed notes, which constrains the dividend through the distributable-reserves test.
  5. Floating-rate exposure has roughly doubled and the sign of the rate sensitivity has flipped. At 31 December 2025 a +100bp move produced +$23m of interest expense against +$57m of interest income, so higher rates helped net finance expense by $34m. At 30 June 2026 floating liabilities are about $5.2bn [estimate: swapped-to-floating debt plus commercial paper plus overdrafts; the interim split is not disclosed] against $4,968m of floating assets, so the direction has reversed.
  6. Lease growth: $945m in six months with $354m still to arrive, non-discretionary and easy to miss because it is non-cash on recognition.
  7. Pension: a $999m deficit on a $114bn balance sheet with the hedging described above.

13.3 What drove the decade

The decade is two regimes with a loss-of-exclusivity trough between them.

FY2015–FY2018 FY2018–FY2021 FY2021–FY2025
Total Revenue 24,708 → 22,090 (−3.7%/yr) 22,090 → 37,417 (+19.2%/yr) 37,417 → 58,739 (+12.0%/yr)
Operating profit 4,114 → 3,387 3,387 → 1,056 1,056 → 13,743
What moved Crestor, Nexium, Seroquel and Symbicort exclusivity: Other Disease Areas Product Sales −46% and the cardio-metabolic franchise −29%, against Oncology +113% The Alexion acquisition plus Vaxzevria; Oncology +115% Oncology +83%, Rare Disease full-year effect, Vaxzevria unwind (Vaccines & Immune Therapies Product Sales $4,665m → $846m)

Only one acquisition in eleven years changed the growth rate. Cash paid for subsidiaries net of cash acquired was $9,263m in FY2021 plus $2,779m of net borrowings acquired and about 236m shares issued; every other year was $0–2,771m of bolt-ons. Of the $6,934m of FY2022 Total Revenue growth, $3,943m — 57% — was the Alexion annualisation [estimate: the $3,943m is Product Sales and the $6,934m is Total Revenue, so treat 57% as approximate]. FY2023–FY2025 growth is organic: cash acquisitions were $48m, an undisclosed FY2023 figure, $2,771m for two clinical-stage companies with no revenue, and $66m.

Where the margin came from, year by year.

Year Gross % Operating % Driver
FY2016 82.1 21.3 Revenue −6.9% but operating profit +19%: Other operating income $1,655m and a $1,699m cut in selling and administrative expense
FY2017 80.8 16.4 Intangible impairment $491m; selling and administrative back up $820m

FY2025 81.9 23.4 Highest reported operating margin of the eleven years. Impairment declined to $230m and restructuring to $237m; selling and administrative held flat in dollars on +9% revenue

Every point of margin expansion has been commercial-cost dilution rather than research efficiency, computed in Section 1.4. Alliance Revenue went from $755m (FY2022) to $3,067m (FY2025), +39% in FY2025 and +34% in Q2 2026. Because it is a share of a partner's gross profit its gross margin is roughly 100%, mechanically lifting reported Gross Margin, while the FY2025 Financial Review names "negative product mix effects from rising contributions of products with share of gross profit arrangements" as a drag. Both mechanisms are live, and the reported line moved up 1 point to 82% in the same table that names the drag. And Collaboration Revenue declined 89% from $923m to $99m in FY2025 because the FY2024 figure included a $600m Lynparza sales milestone, which is $824m off the reported revenue line and not a business decline.

Reported return on invested capital was below 11% in six of the eleven years and only reached 16.0% in FY2025, against Core return of 21.0%; the gap is intangible amortisation, and cumulative amortisation plus impairment over FY2016–FY2025 was $33,460m against cumulative cash purchases of intangible assets of $15,379m. Free cash flow to EBITDA peaked at 0.94x in FY2022 and has declined to 0.60x, because property capital expenditure went from $1,091m to $2,810m and capital commitments from $502m to $1,727m. Days of inventory on cost of sales were 225 in FY2025 against 189 in FY2024, and the cash conversion cycle has ranged from 130 to 275 days across the decade, so there is no working-capital trend to build into a forward case. Share-based payment was 1.2% of Total Revenue in FY2025 and does not dilute because awards are settled with market-purchased shares.

Disposal gains no longer support the operating line. Over FY2015–FY2019 Other operating income and expense averaged $1,811m a year against average operating profit of $3,801m — 48% of operating profit came from disposal gains and milestone income, peaking at 75% in FY2018 on $2,338m of intangible disposals. In FY2024 and FY2025 the line was $252m and $381m, 2.5–2.8% of operating profit, with intangible-disposal proceeds of $123m and $136m. The reported profit-and-loss statement no longer has that source of income.

Any model taking FY2025's +8% CER growth, 23.4% Reported operating margin, +2% CER cardio-renal franchise or +4% CER China as the current state is six to twelve months stale on all four.▪

14. Expectations: internal, external and base rates

The disagreement is about margin. Consensus takes management's $80bn 2030 revenue ambition essentially at face value — $80,594m against $80bn — and then goes further than management on margin, at a 38.0% Core operating margin in FY2030 against a company commitment of "at least mid-30s%".▪ The only place the street declines to take management's number is the current year, where consensus revenue implies about +5.7% CER against a guided mid-to-high single digit.

Driver Internal (management) External (consensus, 7 Aug 2026) Where and why they disagree Base rate
Total Revenue, FY2026 +5% to +9% CER ("mid-to-high single-digit"), reconfirmed 27 July 2026 $63,275m, +7.7% actual; about +5.7% CER after a 2pp FX benefit (n=28, high–low 4.3% of mean) The street disbelieves 1–2 points of the revenue guide while accepting the earnings guide. H1 delivered +6% CER and Q2 +5% CER, so the guide requires H2 at roughly +6% to +12% CER with the Farxiga drag moving from partial to full period AstraZeneca met or beat its initial revenue guidance in nine consecutive completed years with no full-year cut on the eleven-year record. Class median one-year growth +2% to +4%
Total Revenue, 2030 $80bn, risk-adjusted, explicitly assuming no future M&A; implies +6.4%/yr $80,594m, +6.5%/yr (n=15, high–low 24.0% of mean, $71,394m to $90,767m). Named: Leerink $80.8bn, Guggenheim $78.0bn They are effectively the same number, so the mean is not independent evidence. The CFO's own datapoint: consensus moved from $67bn when the target was set to about $76bn by mid-2025 to $80bn now 96th percentile. 3 of 80 five-year windows from a $45bn-plus base cleared +6.4%, all Pfizer (two the same COVID window, one Wyeth). Median +1.3%, p90 +5.3%. Over ten years, 0 of 57 windows cleared it. Requires $21,261m of net new revenue against a median five-year addition of $3,223m

Not restated on either 2026 call 33.0% (FY2026E), 34.3%, 35.3%, 36.0%, 38.0% (FY2030E) Consensus has absorbed a two-year delay against a target management has not restated, then goes above it in the outer year. Neither is the FY2025 actual of 31.5% Median −3.8pp over five years from a 28–36% start (n=33), with only 18% of windows holding or expanding. The joint test of +6% revenue with +400bp of margin from a $45bn-plus base has one precedent in 80 windows
Core EPS, FY2026 +10% to +13% ("low double-digit"), reconfirmed twice $10.27, +12.1% (n=27) Squarely inside the guided band. H1 delivered +11% CER Nine of nine years met or beat; the one scoreable miss was FY2019

Gross margin "stable to slightly higher" than 2025; lower in H2 on FluMist seasonality 82.3% (FY2026E) rising to 82.7% (FY2030E) — a 40bp move across five years with no visible dispersion Not a debate. The three dapagliflozin combinations read out H1 2027 with a company peak guide of "almost $10 billion" that BofA states consensus has "basically nothing" for The most explicitly unmodelled driver in the whole consensus, in both directions AZN's own 2011–2016 loss-of-exclusivity cohort ran −60% excluding FX over five years; Brilinta −38% in year one and 1.1% of pre-loss US revenue five quarters later

Post-2030 revenue "sustained growth thereafter" Nothing exists. Bloomberg has no FY2031-plus estimates The Imfinzi (2031), Tagrisso (2032) and Calquence (2032) expiries covering 28.7% of FY2025 Total Revenue fall entirely outside the published horizon. The absence is symmetrical: the street models neither the cliff nor the replacement —
Buyback suspended since 2012, suspension reaffirmed in the FY2025 Annual Report not modelled — Fourteen years of nothing

AstraZeneca hits its annual guidance and misses its multi-year targets. Across FY2016–FY2025 and two guided metrics, AstraZeneca beat 9 times, met inside the band 10 times and missed once — FY2019 Core EPS at $3.46 on the guided budget-rate basis against a guided $3.50–3.70, where the Annual Report leads with the $3.50 actual-FX figure and does not state that the guided basis was missed. Every guidance revision in eleven years was upward, and there is no full-year cut on the record: not in 2020, not in 2021, not in 2023 when COVID-19 revenue declined sharply, and not in 2026. Sandbagging was material in four of ten years: 2017, 2022, 2023 and 2024 were beaten by 5 to 12 percentage points. In the other six it was absent.

FY2025 was the first year since FY2020 with no upward revision at any quarter, and it landed at the exact centre of the revenue band and the bottom third of the EPS band.▪ The sequence into the current year is 9M 2025 +11% CER, Q4 2025 +2%, Q1 2026 +8%, Q2 2026 +5%. Against multi-year targets there are two data points and both are weak: the 2014 $45bn-by-2023 ambition was met on the headline and missed organically, and the mid-30s-margin-by-2026 target has not moved in three years and no longer carries a date.

What management is willing to guide has narrowed steadily. In FY2016–FY2017 it guided Total Revenue and Core EPS percentages plus research and selling-cost direction plus a tax range; in FY2018–FY2019 it used a dollar Core EPS range, the most falsifiable form in the record and the only construction that produced a scoreable miss; in FY2022–FY2023 it added explicit China and Emerging Markets numbers plus line-item direction; from FY2024 it guides Total Revenue and Core EPS percentages and the Core tax rate, and nothing else. The dollar range has not been used since FY2021 and the China number was withdrawn in the year China turned sharply negative.

HSBC, Guggenheim and Leerink all cut after the CARDIO-TTRansform failure; UBS, writing before it, argued the pipeline replaces what the cliff takes. HSBC cut to Hold with a 13,750p target on 13 July 2026 after the CARDIO-TTRansform failure, arguing the path to $80bn is "increasingly dependent on future clinical milestones that carry greater execution risk", that it is "rather uncomfortable" with both H2 2026 readouts, and that "if three trials fail in a sequence, the widely held view of Astra's market-leading R&D platform might lose its shine" — a bear case about the research platform's credibility, and still 15.6% above spot (Yahoo Finance, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. Guggenheim, eleven days later, characterises investor expectations for the same two readouts as "very low" and cut its 2030 forecast to $78.0bn; Leerink puts 20% probability on SERENA-4 and 50% on AVANZAR and cut 2030 to $80.8bn from $82.7bn, implying the failed Wainua indication had been worth about $1.9bn of 2030 revenue (BioSpace, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. UBS, before those events, argued AstraZeneca has "sector leading replacement power" and quantified the option at $17.2bn of incremental 2030 revenue if the current late-stage pipeline moved to 100% probability of success (Proactive Investors, accessed 2026-08-07) [web]. Bloomberg records 36 analysts at 30 buy / 4 hold / 2 sell with a 15,286 GBp consensus target, and the identity and current argument of the two sellers could not be established because the only retrievable Deutsche Bank note is dated August 2024.

Dispersion widens with horizon: revenue high-to-low as a share of the mean runs 4.3% (FY2026), 13.0%, 11.8%, 16.7% and 24.0% (FY2030), with contributors falling from 28 to 15. FY2026 is settled. The disagreement is all in 2028–2030 and it is about pipeline outcomes, not the base business, because the gross-margin assumption is a straight line every contributor agrees on. That leaves research and selling intensity as the residual disagreement on earnings, which is the question BofA asked on the Q2 2026 call; management declined to answer it for 2027, deferring to the FY2026 results.

15. Market pricing and valuation history

This section contains no valuation judgment. Where a cited source makes one it is attributed to that source.

All price levels, returns, drawdowns and session reactions are measured on the London ordinary line, the primary listing and the only continuous eleven-year series, with multiples converted at the same-date GBPUSD rate; the pre-February-2026 US series is an American Depositary Share series at two shares to one ordinary share, and Bloomberg's US price history, already retroactively adjusted for the conversion, tracks the dollar-ordinary series within 0.5–1.4% at every test date.

The two halves of the decade are opposites.

From 2015 to 2019 the price rose 48% while Core earnings declined 18%, so every dollar of that move and more was the multiple: the market paid an extra 80% per unit of earnings for a company whose revenue was declining. From 2019 to 2025 the reverse: earnings compounded at 17.4% a year and the multiple declined 30%. Of the +173% ten-year price move, 115 points came from Core EPS and 27 points from the multiple, and the multiple's entire contribution came in the first four years against declining earnings, then partly reversed.

The Alexion close added $8.2bn of goodwill and $21.5bn of intangibles, taking equity from $15,622m to $39,268m and mechanically halving price-to-book from 8.4x to 4.6x with no change in the business, so the series records an accounting event.

AstraZeneca beat the stored consensus in 8 of the 10 events where one exists, missed twice, and both misses were inside half a percent; the median surprise is about +1.2% and only two prints are outside ±4%, both first quarters. The surprise does not explain the reaction. The largest beat of the twelve, +10.2% in Q1 2025, produced +0.9%; the larger of the two misses, −0.5% for FY2023, produced −6.4%; a −0.2% miss for FY2025 produced +2.0%. Two of the three reactions beyond ±5% came on surprises of +0.4% and −0.5%.

Quarter Reaction What the market reacted to
FY2023 (2024-02-08) −6.4% The FY2024 guidance implied flat operating margin against a mid-30s commitment. An analyst put it to management directly on the call: "the top line guidance is about the same pace as the bottom line guidance. So that would imply then that margins might be about flat… does that mean margins will be flat this year and then have to have a big inflection in '25 and '26 to get there?" Management also guided FY2024 to "a slightly lower product sales gross margin percentage". EPS itself was in line at −0.5%

FY2024 (2025-02-06) +5.9% Guidance and dividend, not the print (+0.4%). Management issued FY2025 guidance of "total revenue to increase by a high single-digit percentage and core EPS to increase by low double-digit percentage" and raised the payout: "We increased the full year 2024 dividend to $3.10 per share and announced this morning that we intend to increase our full year 2025 dividend to $3.20." It landed three months after the China-probe drawdown with the shares at 11,126p against a 13,276p September-2024 high. The margin news in the same release was negative — "We were probably expecting margin to end at around 32% in '24 and ended just above 31%" — and the market bought it anyway

Six of the eleven largest single sessions of the decade were clinical or regulatory news with no earnings content, and only one — Q3 2021 — was an earnings miss large enough to move the price by itself. The earnings-surprise distribution is about ±4% while the readout-driven sessions run ±6% to ±15%.

Bloomberg's own currency-consistent forward price-to-earnings gives 15.637x, 14.005x and 12.620x for FY2026–FY2028, matching the computation above to 0.01x. Consensus FY2030 revenue is $80,594m against management's $80bn ambition, on only 12 contributing earnings estimates. And the gap between Core and IFRS earnings narrows steadily across the forecast — Core EPS stands 40% above IFRS EPS in FY2025 actual, 34% in FY2026E, 26% in FY2027E and 22% in FY2028E — so consensus assumes the amortisation and impairment gap shrinks, while the Q2 2026 actual moved the other way, with depreciation, amortisation and impairment up 39% to $1,928m.

On the twelve-month-forward blended consensus Core EPS across 140 monthly observations from December 2014, the forward price-to-earnings has a median of 17.8x, an interquartile range of 15.9x–19.0x, a low of 13.5x (30 November 2016) and a high of 23.7x (31 December 2019). The latest monthly print is 15.5x (31 July 2026); using the 7 August price with that earnings figure gives 14.6x. The 2026 path was 18.0x at end-December 2025, 20.0x at end-February, 17.1x at end-June and 15.5x at end-July.

Bloomberg returned no high, low or standard-deviation field for forward earnings, so only contributor counts are available. Bloomberg's consensus target price is 15,286 GBp and its analyst rating 4.53 on a 1-to-5 scale, and there is no AstraZeneca coverage at all in the local sell-side digest to corroborate or dispute them.

The Farxiga loss of exclusivity and Chinese procurement are real and in the numbers, and they are not what drove the shares down 26% from the February high, because consensus rose through the drawdown rather than falling. The twelve-month-forward Core EPS estimate went from $10.304 at end-December 2025 to $10.497 at end-February to $10.977 at end-July 2026, and FY2026 guidance was reconfirmed unchanged on 27 July. So the decline is the multiple: forward price-to-earnings 18.0x to 15.5x from December to July (−13.9%) while forward earnings rose 6.5%, and 20.0x to 15.5x from late February (−22.2%) while forward earnings rose 4.6%. The two largest single legs were the CARDIO-TTRansform failure on 9 July and the reported Bristol Myers merger talks on 3 August, neither of which touched the FY2026 estimate.

Merck's FY2026E is a charge year rather than a de-rating: consensus FY2026E adjusted EPS of $2.77 against $8.94 in FY2025 actual, with FY2027E back to $9.58 and FY2026E EBITDA halving, so the 46x price-to-earnings and 25x enterprise-value-to-EBITDA are artefacts of acquired in-process research expensing inside the estimate year. Its three-month and one-year FY2026E revisions are −43.4% and −71.2%, the largest in the universe. Currency: EPS is each issuer's reporting currency and the price is its primary-listing quote, and for AstraZeneca those differ (dollar earnings, pence price). All price-to-earnings and enterprise-value-to-EBITDA cells come from Bloomberg's currency-consistent calculation, validated against an independent computation to 0.0% on 29 of 32 rows. Blanks: Apellis has no Bloomberg market capitalisation or enterprise value; Roche, AbbVie, argenx and BeOne have no price-to-book; Roche's FY2025 adjusted EPS came back off a single contributor and was blanked as stale rather than shown; Gilead, Moderna and Apellis have negative or near-zero FY2026E earnings and show n/m.

17. Forward model summary

No valuation.

The model is built at the medicine level. Note 7 states one reportable segment, so there is no segment operating profit to forecast and no segment margin to extrapolate, while each individual medicine has a disclosed revenue by region, a disclosed patent-expiry date by market and, where exclusivity has already gone, an observed erosion rate. Revenue is therefore 41 medicine paths plus a probability-weighted pipeline bucket, summed into the therapy areas and then into the group; no line is a top-down revenue growth rate. Year 0 is FY2025 tied exactly to the reported accounts, and FY2026 starts from H1 2026 actuals rather than from a full-year growth rate: H1 Total Revenue of $30,672m as reported plus a driver-built H2 of $32,185m, which is +4.9% on H2 2025's $30,694m, giving FY2026 of $62,857m or +5.0% CER after deducting the guided low-single-digit FX benefit, which is the floor of the reconfirmed guidance band and 0.7% below consensus.
