17.2 The loss-of-exclusivity schedule the model applies

The erosion rates are AstraZeneca's own: Crestor US −57% on about seven months of exposure; Brilinta US $751m to $393m to $2m, 1.1% of the pre-loss level five quarters after entry; Soliris −29% actual in year one with Europe −50% CER; Farxiga US −48% actual in the first full generic quarter; and the FY2016 Annual Report's own Established-Markets cohort at $20bn to $6bn, −70% actual and −60% excluding FX.

Cohort Medicines FY2025 revenue $m Modelled outcome, base
Already eroding or expiring by 2027 Farxiga 8,492, Symbicort 2,885, Soliris 1,837, Lynparza 3,279, Brilinta 823, roxadustat 276 17,592 = 29.9% of Total Revenue FY2029E $6,128m (−65%); FY2035E $3,642m (−79%). Bear FY2029E $4,358m (−75%); bull $8,889m (−49%)
2030–2035, outside every published forecast Imfinzi 6,063, Tagrisso 7,254, Calquence 3,518, Enhertu 2,775 19,610 FY2030E $28,860m → FY2035E $9,760m, −66%

Bloomberg has 15 revenue contributors for FY2030 and none beyond, so the entire second cohort falls outside the published consensus horizon, which is why the model runs to FY2035.

17.3 Assumptions and where each is contested

The 27 drivers are in workpapers\model_assumptions.json with bear, base and bull, unit, source and one-line justification. Two of the 27 are refuted by the evidence and most of the rest are weak on range rather than on level.

Driver Bear Base Bull Source Where the assumption is contested
Pipeline risk-adjusted peak-year revenue $22.6bn $37.0bn $56.5bn Base rate Weak. The 55% probability applied uniformly is the Phase III chain (52.4% published, about 60% management-stated), but Cohort C — $14.0bn of the $37.0bn — is defined as Phase III readouts in 2029–2032 and by construction is not in Phase III today; the correct chain for a Phase II asset is 15.1%, so 55% overstates by about 3.5x on that tranche. Re-risking gives $26.8bn, close to the bear. Against that, the portfolio is biomarker-selected, where published Phase I likelihood is 15.9% against 7.6% without. This is the largest swing in the table: $5,766m of FY2032 Core operating profit and $4,085m of FY2030 revenue
Small-molecule loss-of-exclusivity depth 1.20x 1.00x 0.80x Historical record Holds. The base is the company's own realised curve (−48% to −57% in year one, about 1% of pre-loss US revenue by year two) rather than a judgment about it. The asymmetry is that the bull at 0.80x is softer than anything AstraZeneca has printed and the bear is nearly inert once erosion already runs to −98%. Second-largest sensitivity at $2,493m of FY2032 Core operating profit
Biologic loss-of-exclusivity depth 1.25x 1.00x 0.75x Historical record Weak. The base is Soliris's −29% year one, which AstraZeneca partly produced by converting patients to its own Ultomiris — Imfinzi, Enhertu and Fasenra have no equivalent internal successor. And Soliris Europe was −50% CER in H1 2026 against US −27%, so 1.25x on a −29% base does not contain AstraZeneca's own worst realised biologic erosion, which implies 1.72x. Evidence supports a base near 1.3x, a bear near 1.7x and regional differentiation. The four medicines were $19,610m of FY2025 revenue
Baxdrostat FY2035 revenue $1.85bn $4.98bn $6.70bn Management guidance Refuted, on two grounds. Management's guide is more than $5bn peak-year revenue across monotherapy plus the dapagliflozin combinations [deck: ESC 2025, slide 29], and the model assigns $4,980m to the monotherapy alone while separately placing the three combinations inside the pipeline bucket, so the same $5bn is counted roughly twice. And the ramp has no precedent in AstraZeneca's own launch record: Baxfendy booked $3m in H1 2026, has no Medicare Part D reimbursement until 2028 in what the Chief Commercial Officer calls a highly dominated Part D population, and competes against $4 generic antihypertensives without an outcomes trial. Recent launches at FY2025: Lokelma $698m in about year 8, Saphnelo $686m in about year 5, Wainua $212m, Airsupra $166m; Farxiga itself took eleven years to $8.4bn. Evidence supports roughly $1.0–1.5bn by 2030 and $2.5–3.5bn by FY2035 for the monotherapy alone. Third-largest sensitivity: $2,358m of FY2032 Core operating profit and $2,812m of FY2030 revenue
Net finance expense, FY2030 $2,600m $1,950m $1,600m Judgment Refuted. Arithmetically inconsistent with the model's own balance sheet: FY2025 net finance expense of $1,334m on net debt of $23,374m is a 5.7% cost, and the base takes the expense +46% to $1,950m by FY2030 while taking net debt −55% to $10,576m, an implied 18.4% cost on net debt; by FY2035 it charges $2,101m against net cash of $3,046m. Whichever way $12.8bn of net-debt reduction happens the answer is lower. The refinancing step-up is real but small — the sub-2.5%-coupon 2028–2031 tranche repriced to about 4.5% adds roughly $150m a year rather than $616m, the two 2026 maturities were repaid rather than refinanced, and the long end is already above market. Evidence supports FY2030 net finance expense of roughly $0.9–1.4bn, worth about $0.41 of FY2030 Core EPS, about 3.7% of the model's $11.02
Oncology growth 0.78x 1.00x 1.20x Judgment Weak on range. The base level survives — the base-rate band is +4% to +9%/yr, Imfinzi's realised Medicare record is +12.7%/yr beneficiaries, and Q2 2026 realised +15% CER — but the bear at 0.78x still gives +4.9%/yr and contemplates none of the three named threats: Calquence's Maximum Fair Price on 1 January 2027, the loss of the BTK class revenue lead, and MARIPOSA at +124% growth. A bear that contemplated them is nearer 0.35x
Tagrisso path flat +1.2%/yr to $7,700m by FY2030 re-accelerates Judgment Weak. A plus-or-minus 11% band on 12.4% of group Total Revenue facing a funded challenger. Rybrevant and Lazcluze grew +124% off $734m in a pool where Tagrisso holds 90.8%; at 40%/yr they reach about $4.0bn by 2030, taking Tagrisso's share to about 65% and its revenue to about $6.6bn, below the bear's flat case. The range should run roughly 0.70x–1.10x
Farxiga EU generic entry 2027 2028 2029 Management guidance Weak, and immaterial. The base takes a Q4 2025 call statement on a patent family a UK court held invalid in April 2025, upheld on appeal in July 2025 with Supreme Court permission denied, and now challenged in France, Poland and Portugal with interim injunctions obtained in Poland in January 2026. On that evidence the base should be 2027 and the bear 2026. It stops short of refuted only on materiality: the driver moves FY2030 revenue by $325m, the smallest of the 27, because what determines the outcome is terminal retained share (1.1% in the US, about 16% in Europe on Brilinta) rather than the entry date
China procurement-exposed lines 0.72x 1.00x 1.22x Judgment Weak. The base's stated precedent — the post-procurement retail brand annuity, analogised to Crestor and Betaloc — is contradicted by the model's own decomposition, in which those lines subtracted from FY2023–FY2025 growth (Section 6.1). And the scalar covers only three lines (roxadustat $274m, Pulmicort $518m, Farxiga China to $415m by 2030) against a China book of $6,654m, 11.3% of group, while group China ran +4% CER to −13% CER. The driver is also unfalsifiable as specified, because AstraZeneca does not split China revenue between procurement-exposed off-patent originator and reimbursement-listed patented medicine
Rare Disease growth ×0.85 +1.6%/yr to $9,860m by FY2030 ×1.15 Judgment Weak. The 7%/yr fall in revenue per patient driving the base is a single observation from one Investor Day slide extrapolated for ten years, and +1.6% is at the bottom of a 0% to +8%/yr band while the two medicines that are 70% of the franchise compound at about 20% and the realised H1 2026 rate is +11% CER. Counter-evidence that stops this being refuted: the indication-expansion case has demonstrably failed, and Soliris at $1,837m and −29% is a real drag. Evidence supports 0.8x–1.35x
Respiratory & Immunology growth ×0.85 +4.8%/yr to $11,215m by FY2030 ×1.15 Judgment Weak. The stated basis is factually wrong on one input: it claims respiratory biologics and the triple class are the only part of BioPharmaceuticals with both structural volume growth and post-2030 exclusivity, while the model's own biologic-erosion driver puts Fasenra at 2029 and Fasenra is 22% of the franchise; Symbicort is a further 33% and eroding; and RESOLUTE missed, removing the largest indication expansion. Tezspire's US economics belong to Amgen, so its +45% headline converts to AstraZeneca revenue at a fraction
Pipeline cannibalisation retained 0.75 0.85 0.92 Judgment Weak, and double-counted in one direction. The model already flattens Imfinzi from 2029 and declines it from 2031 for next-generation immuno-oncology cannibalisation and says so, so a further 15% haircut on the pipeline bucket for the same mechanism counts it twice. Conversely the dapagliflozin-combination leg is close to empty, because by the time the combinations launch there is very little branded dapagliflozin left to cannibalise. Either Imfinzi holds the cannibalisation and the base should be about 0.95, or the bucket does and Imfinzi should not also flatten. $1,365m of FY2032 Core operating profit
US gross-to-net, FY2030 56.0% 54.0% 51.0% Judgment Weak on the terminal. The single realised year-on-year move was 3.8 points, with chargebacks up 66% over two years, and the base assumes that decelerates to 0.9pp/yr immediately and then goes flat after 2030. No disclosed year supports that plateau. The base survives because the Part D redesign step is now annualised, making 3.8pp a level shift rather than a rate, and because the Maximum Fair Prices and most-favoured-nation pricing are in separate drivers. The bear should run to about 58%
Most-favoured-nation haircut on new launches 12% 6% 2% Judgment Weak. Nothing supports 6%: management concedes the policy is a 2026 headwind and refuses to size it. The observable US-to-lowest-OECD gap on branded medicines is a 50–70% price differential, so a 6% revenue haircut requires either very little new-launch volume in scope or offsetting access gains, and neither is evidenced. Because the scope is new products, it applies to the entire $21.3bn increment and to essentially none of the base. Evidence supports widening to roughly 2–25% and labelling it unknown rather than uncertain. Tenth-largest swing at $1,177m
Gross margin delta −1.2pp 0.0pp on a path of 83.0% (FY2026) to 84.0% (FY2029–30) then 82.5% (FY2035) +0.8pp Historical record Weak. The path peaks 1.9 points above the eleven-year record high of 82.1% (FY2016) and AstraZeneca is already above the 90th percentile of the $25bn-plus class, whose median is 69.9%. The bear never declines below the FY2025 actual, even though the model's own FY2035 mix has Oncology at 23.7% of revenue against 49.5% in FY2030, wholly owned conjugates with full cost of goods replacing roughly 100%-margin alliance revenue, and the $50bn onshoring programme raising unit production cost. Not refuted because the caption was redefined effective 1 January 2025 so pre-2025 comparisons do not bind, and the near-term path starts from reported actuals with two disclosed mechanical tailwinds
Core R&D % of revenue delta +1.0pp 0.0pp on a path of 23.5% to FY2027, easing to 22.5% from FY2031 −1.0pp Management guidance Weak. Every restatement of the commitment has moved up: "low-20s%" at Investor Day became "the upper end of the low 20s range" at the FY2025 results and again on the Q2 2026 call, and FY2025 Core research was 23.5%. The terminal years require a nominal dollar cut with no precedent — from $16,080m (FY2030) to $14,734m (FY2035), −8.4% nominal over five years, whereas reported research has declined in only two of eleven years and never for more than two consecutive years. And the bear at 24.5% is roughly the FY2017–FY2019 realised level, so it is not bearish
Core SG&A growth, FY2027 5.5% 4.0% 2.0% Judgment Weak. H1 2026 realised +6% CER, so FY2027 at +4.0% requires an immediate 2-point deceleration in the year Baxfendy still has no Part D reimbursement, the freed US primary-care field force is being held and redeployed at full cost, and nine further new medicines must launch by 2030. AstraZeneca's own launch-wave precedent ran the other way at +16.5% in FY2019. Counterweight: in the last trough it cut selling and administrative expense −15.3% in one year, far more than the model's response rule permits, so the path's rise to 30.5% of revenue by FY2035 may overstate the back-end cost base. The range brackets neither precedent
Other operating income from FY2027 $350m $500m $850m Historical record Weak on range. The line ran $1,500m to $381m across FY2015–FY2025 and the FY2015–FY2019 average of $1,811m is correct, as is the mechanism. But the bear of $350m is 39% above FY2024's realised $252m, so the band does not contain an observation from two years ago. The line has re-accelerated to $341m in H1 2026 with a similar second half guided, so stepping down to $500m is a real haircut. The bear should extend to about $250m. $500m of FY2032 Core operating profit
Intangible amortisation delta +$500m $0 on a schedule of $4.6–4.7bn to FY2029 stepping down to $2.9bn by FY2035 −$500m Historical record Weak. The schedule steps down as the Alexion launched-product tranche exhausts, while the same model spends $5,200m in FY2026 then $3,500m a year on intangible purchases, cumulatively $36,700m by FY2035, on a line that has already compounded from $294m (FY2017) to $3,095m (FY2025) while amortisation followed from $1,999m to $4,207m. Even if only half the forward spend is launched product on a ten-year life, the additions generate more than $1.8bn of annual amortisation by the early 2030s. The partial defence is that much of the spend is milestone payments on unapproved assets held as non-amortising in-process research until approval, and the model gives no split. Reported-basis only, $206m of FY2032 all-in free cash flow
Net intangible impairment $1,400m $600m/yr $250m Historical record Weak. The ten-year mean is computed on eight disclosed observations because FY2020–FY2022 are not tagged, and those three years span the Alexion acquisition and the COVID-19 portfolio. The bear does not contain the worst observed year, FY2024's $1,574m. And exposure scales with the intangible book, which is being added to at $3,095m (FY2025) and $3,333m in H1 2026 alone, with $355m of research impairment already booked in H1 2026. Evidence supports a base of roughly $700–800m rising with the book and a bear of roughly $1,800m
Restructuring $900m $500m/yr $250m Historical record Weak. The eleven-year mean is $736m and the bear of $900m is below both of the two worst years ($1,283m FY2021, $1,154m FY2024) and below the FY2015–FY2017 programme run-rate. The bear's own stated mechanism — that the exclusivity wave forces a primary-care restructuring programme — is precisely what produced $1,034m and $1,107m in the last trough. Evidence supports a base near $700m and a bear near $1,200m
Core tax rate 22.5% 20.0% average FY2026–35 18.5% Management guidance Holds. The realised reported effective rate printed below 20% in eight of eleven years including 17.5% in FY2025, so a base drifting to 21.35% by FY2035 on Pillar Two and a rising US mix is above the realised rate throughout, and the bear is above the top of the guided 18–22% band. The Q2 2026 rate benefited from a one-time deferred-tax adjustment, which the model excludes
Capex % of revenue 7.5% 5.8% FY2027–30 average 4.8% Judgment Weak, and internally inconsistent on the FY2026 base. The justification applies the Q2 2026 guide of capital expenditure increasing by around one third to FY2025's $3,270m, which gives about $4.4bn against the model's FY2026 of $3,700m, which is $2,810m times 1.32, so one of the two base figures is wrong and the gap is about $660m a year. And 5.8% exists only in FY2015–FY2017, before the $50bn US programme, the $4.5bn Charlottesville plant and the $2bn Maryland expansion; if even 40% of the $50bn is manufacturing capital expenditure across FY2026–30 that is about $4bn a year of US spend alone, nearer the bear's 7.5%. Counterweight: H1 2026 capital expenditure of $1.5bn annualises below the modelled $3,700m. $936m of FY2032 all-in free cash flow and $8,379m of FY2032 net debt
Purchase of intangible assets from FY2027 $5,000m $3,500m/yr ($5,200m in FY2026) $2,500m Historical record Weak on the individual line, sound on the total. FY2026 is already blown: intangible purchases were $3,333m in H1 2026 alone, annualising near $6,666m against a modelled $5,200m, so holding FY2026 requires a 44% half-on-half decline in a year that has already produced the CSPC, Dizal and CTTQ transactions. And the FY2027 reversion breaks an eleven-year trend that rose in eight of the last nine years. On the aggregate it holds: $3,500m of intangibles plus $700m of contingent consideration plus $1,000m of acquisitions is $5,200m a year against a revealed thirty-month cadence of about $4.8bn a year. Largest net-debt swing at $15,000m of FY2032 net debt, with zero effect on operating profit
Working capital absorbed per incremental revenue dollar 25% 20% (plus a $1.9bn FY2026 Farxiga deferral) 15% Historical record Weak on calibration, immaterial in effect. 20% is below both recent readings: FY2025 absorbed $1,137m on $4,666m of revenue growth, 24%, and H1 2026 absorbed $1,438m with the Farxiga right-of-return drag guided to persist. Holding days of sales, inventory and payables flat for ten years is a strong simplification against a realised cash conversion cycle that has ranged from 130 to 275 days. The driver moves FY2032 all-in free cash flow by $0 because the floor applies once growth slows
Dividend per share growth from FY2027 0% (held at $3.30) +3.5%/yr +6.0% Historical record Holds. The eleven-year realised rate is 1.35% with six consecutive flat years, so on the long record the bear is the better central case. But the last three declarations were +6.9%, +3.2% and +3.1%, so 3.5% is the current run-rate, and affordability is not binding in the base case: cover on Core EPS never declines below 1.93x and $60bn of dividends compares with $95bn of cumulative all-in free cash flow. The bear reproduces the FY2015–FY2020 regime exactly, so the range brackets both observed policies
Share repurchases $0 $0 $3,000m/yr from FY2029 Historical record Holds. Fourteen years of evidence supports zero: no repurchases since 2012, the suspension repeated verbatim in the FY2025 Annual Report, five reporting periods since the CFO's "consider and think about buybacks" remark with nothing following, and employee awards settled with market-purchased shares at roughly $0.9bn a year of cash rather than by issuance. The incoherence a zero base creates — $95bn of cumulative free cash flow, net debt retired by FY2033, FY2035 net cash of $3,046m and no disclosed use — is a defect in the net-finance driver rather than in this one

The bear case does not manage its balance sheet: bear net debt goes $27.0bn (FY2026) to $42.4bn (FY2030) to $61.8bn (FY2035), or 7.1x EBITDA, because the capital-discipline rule cuts capital expenditure and business development from FY2032 but does not cut the dividend: the bear holds dividend per share at $3.30 for ten years, costing $51bn against $21bn of cumulative all-in free cash flow. That is the 2015–2020 pattern reproduced at larger scale — in that period dividends were $21,214m against operating cash flow of $21,433m, the dividend consumed 99%, 135% and 121% of operating cash flow in FY2017–FY2019, dividend per share was held at $2.80 for nine years, and net debt rose $8.9bn. The model does not impose a cut because "progressive" is a no-cut commitment the Board has never broken, and imposing one would flatter the bear case.

Pipeline probability of success is the largest swing at $5.8bn of FY2032 Core operating profit, a quarter of base-case Core operating profit, and every other pipeline judgment feeds into it. The Farxiga European entry year barely matters ($325m of FY2030 revenue) while the small-molecule erosion depth matters a great deal ($3,725m), so the outcome turns on terminal retained share, not on the European expiry date, and the company's own record is 1.1% in the US and about 16% in Europe five quarters after entry. And capital allocation moves the balance sheet rather than the profit and loss: the dividend-growth and repurchase drivers change FY2032 operating profit by zero and FY2032 net debt by $7.1bn and $11.4bn.

17.6 Where the base case departs from consensus and from management

Consensus Core EPS $ 10.27 11.46 12.72 14.42 16.26

On revenue the model's +3.5% FY2025–30 rate is at roughly the 75th percentile of the reference-class distribution, which is where a company with a real oncology share gain and a large exclusivity cohort should be; consensus and the ambition are at the 96th. On margin the model reaches 33.6% by FY2030 and peaks at 33.7% in FY2031, which is already +2.1 points on FY2025 delivered by mix, not scale, and requires selling and administrative expense growing 3.5–4.0% against revenue growing 2–4%; consensus reaches 38.0%, which maps to roughly 32.5% Reported once amortisation is held near $4.3bn, or +900bp on the reported basis — an outcome that appears in 6 of 104 windows above $25bn of revenue and in no window above $45bn ever.▪ The earnings gap of 32% by FY2030 is the product of those two, and consensus's $16.26 is not an independent estimate.

The FY2026 departure is small. The model gives +5.0% CER revenue, the floor of the band, and +9.7% Core EPS growth, a whisker below the guided low-double-digit, and the reasons are all disclosed by management and all fall in the second half: gross margin guided lower on FluMist seasonality, core finance costs guided higher after refinancing, the Q2 deferred-tax benefit not repeating, and the Farxiga working-capital drag persisting. Against that, AstraZeneca has met or beaten its initial revenue guidance in nine consecutive completed years.

Guggenheim asked on the Q2 2026 call whether the current Phase III pipeline can carry the 2032-plus expiries. The question: "is the current Phase III pipeline sufficient to deliver a stable profile during the main patent expiration period in 2032 plus? It seems to us that the current pressure on the multiple has much less to do with 2030 and much more to do with 2032 and beyond." Soriot: "the answer is no, we don't need [business development] to deliver… this growth post 2030. But again, it assumes that the aggregate probability of success across our pipeline of new products will be at least as we plan it." The model tests that conditional. Tagrisso, Imfinzi, Calquence and Enhertu were $19,610m of FY2025 revenue and reach $28,860m in FY2030; on the disclosed expiry dates and AstraZeneca's own erosion rates they decline to $9,760m by FY2035, −66%. The base-case pipeline bucket adds $24,633m over the same window. The two roughly offset:

FY2030E → FY2035E, base $m
Tagrisso, Imfinzi, Calquence, Enhertu −19,100
other marketed medicines, net −4,197
pipeline bucket, net of cannibalisation +19,890
policy adjustments −1,020
Total Revenue −4,427

So the answer on this model is that the pipeline is roughly sufficient to hold revenue flat through the cliff at a 55% probability of success, and not sufficient to grow through it.▪ The bull case (70% plus a 20% peak uplift) does grow through it to $90.4bn; the bear (42%) gives $47.0bn. One driver produces a $43bn spread, and the base applies a Phase III probability to a tranche that is not yet in Phase III.

The incremental-margin check, and one flagged year. Realised incremental Core operating margins were 35.6% over FY2022–25, 30.5% over FY2023–25, 33.2% in FY2025 and 42.7% in H1 2026. FY2026 is 61%: revenue rises $4,118m while Core operating profit rises $2,507m, and the reason is mix, already visible in the reported numbers, because what left was primary-care revenue at a 92–98% contribution margin and what arrived was Oncology and Rare Disease. FY2027E is 27%, FY2028E 33%, FY2029E 42% and FY2030E 37%, all inside the realised historical range. The bull case exceeds 45% in six consecutive growth years, which is above anything in AstraZeneca's record, and that is the same arithmetic that makes consensus's FY2030 margin hard to reach. The decremental margins of 60–110% in declining years are the correct sign and roughly the right magnitude: exclusivity revenue leaves at a 92–98% contribution margin while the manufacturing estate stays (Section 1.3).

Three contradictions. Two published FY2026 numbers cannot both be right: a low-double-digit Core EPS increase on mid-to-high single-digit revenue growth implies 1–2 points of margin expansion, while the Investor Day target requires 3–4.5 points. The stated position that no business development is needed is contradicted by $2bn of upfronts in seven months. And the $80bn bridge base year has moved between $45.8bn and $54.1bn across successive decks with the endpoint fixed, so the ambition's required growth rate has declined by about 2 points without the ambition changing, while its stated FX basis is deck-only (Appendix A).

18. Risks

Ranked by revenue or profit at stake, by whether it has already begun, and by how soon it arrives. The first four are already realised in reported numbers.

1. Loss of exclusivity is under way on about 26% of Product Sales and the erosion rate matches the peer base rate of roughly −50% in the first year. Mechanism: generic and biosimilar entry removes price and then volume, and in the transition quarters revenue is deferred rather than merely reduced, because AstraZeneca's own policy is that "When a product faces generic competition… in cases where the circumstances are such that the level of Product Sales are considered highly probable to reverse, revenues are only recognised when the right of return expires". Exposure: the loss-of-exclusivity cohort listed in Section 7. Realised so far: Farxiga −19% CER in Q2 2026 with US −48% actual, Brilinta −63% CER, roxadustat −82% CER, Soliris −28% CER, Symbicort −8% CER on a new US generic entrant. Peer base rates: Humira −49% in its third biosimilar year, Revlimid −49% in FY2025, Sprycel −74% over two years, Abraxane −78% in one. Leading indicators, in order of how early each appears:

  • Paragraph-IV filings and settlement dates in Note 30. The Cipla Calquence trial is set for April 2027, and no Lynparza trial date exists against four filers.
  • The European Farxiga patent challenges. The UK patent was invalidated in 2025 and the same family is now challenged in France, Poland and Portugal, with Polish interim injunctions obtained in January 2026. Europe is about 35% of Farxiga revenue and the only region still growing, at +1% CER.
  • Any at-risk launch, which the risk factors note may happen.

2. US policy: a most-favoured-nation regime management concedes is a 2026 headwind, plus a three-year tariff exemption expiring around late 2028, neither quantified anywhere. Three instruments on three different dates. Medicare negotiation: Farxiga's Maximum Fair Price effective 2026 on $1,730m of US revenue and Calquence's effective 2027 on $2,339m, both now administered prices (Section 1.1); AstraZeneca lost its constitutional challenge on Farxiga and filed a new suit in December 2025 challenging the interpretation as applied to Calquence. Most-favoured-nation reference pricing from the October 2025 agreement, unquantified, and confirmed as already repricing a launch product. Section 232 tariffs, deferred three years conditional on onshoring, so the tariff mitigation and the exemption condition are the same thing, because the exemption holds only if the onshoring completes. Exposure: the US was 43% of Q2 2026 Total Revenue and management projects about 50% by 2030. Soriot's framing gives the bound — "it's only for new products, future new products… the whole of Europe represents 20% of our global sales" — and the path from $58,739m to $80bn is a $21.3bn increment from at least 20 new medicines, so essentially the whole increment is priced under the regime and essentially none of the base. Leading indicators: any Section 232 determination or rule text naming pharmaceutical imports; the contractual-rebate line in the next 20-F; the US price and volume split in the Q3 2026 Farxiga and Calquence lines; and capital expenditure against the one-third-increase plan, since a slipping build slips the exemption.

3. US net price: a 50.5% gross-to-net deduction that is a key audit matter, with the government-channel line compounding at twice the rate of gross sales. Both the rate and the accrual are Key Judgements and PwC's first key audit matter, against group materiality of $620m. Chargebacks grew 66% over two years while gross sales grew 30%, and 340B is named zero times in five years of risk factors while three actions run. Contractual managed-care and Medicare rebates rose 29% in FY2025 alone against 16.6% gross-sales growth, the Part D redesign year. The balance-sheet exposure is the accrual: $5,941m carried forward, and a 10% mis-estimation of the $23,941m annual deduction is $2,394m, 17.4% of FY2025 Reported operating profit and 3.9x audit materiality. Leading indicators: the chargebacks line as a percentage of gross in the FY2026 20-F; the prior-year adjustment column in the accrual roll-forward, which was small at $(92)m and $(42)m in FY2025, so a large one would signal estimation strain; and the gross-margin driver list in each 6-K.

4. China: from +4% CER to −13% CER in two quarters, plus a criminal indictment of the local operating entity and its former EVP. Two unrelated exposures in one country that is 11.3% of Total Revenue. Commercially, volume-based procurement puts a medicine to national tender and redistributes volume; Farxiga, Lynparza and roxadustat entered batch 11, implemented in Q1 2026 at mandated cuts of 20%, 30% and 30%, and local competition compounds it. Legally, Note 30 discloses an April 2025 transfer to the prosecutor on suspected unlawful collection of personal information, an October 2025 customs assessment of RMB 24m (about $3.5m) of unpaid import taxes on Imfinzi, Imjudo and Enhertu prepaid as voluntary compensation with a fine of one to five times that amount still possible, and the November 2025 indictment of the entity, its former EVP and a former senior employee, the two individuals additionally on medical-insurance-fraud charges.

5. Pipeline attrition against an ambition that assumes roughly a 60% aggregate Phase III success rate. The $80bn ambition requires at least 20 new medicines by 2030 with 11 approved at H1 2026, and management's stated aggregate probability is around 60% against a published Phase III-to-approval chain of 52.4% and a claimed own record of "75% plus" that has no disclosed denominator. The realised record in the last four quarterly announcements is dense with misses: LATIFY, SAMETA, RESOLUTE, PROSPERO and CARDIO-TTRansform all missed, plus ARTEMIS discontinued and the adult haematopoietic-stem-cell-transplant trial missed. Oncology is at the bottom of the published therapeutic-area distribution (solid tumours at 4.6% likelihood of approval from Phase I against 7.9% all-industry), partly offset by biomarker selection at 15.9% against 7.6%. The two near-term readouts the market is focused on are SERENA-4 and AVANZAR in H2 2026, where the named external probabilities are 20% and 50%.

6. Oncology's two largest medicines lose protection between 2030 and 2032, at the $80bn milestone, and this is the bear case analysts actually put to management. Imfinzi US 2031, Tagrisso US 2032 and 2035, Calquence US 2032–2036 and Enhertu US 2033–2035 were $19,610m of FY2025 revenue and reach $28,860m by FY2030 in the base case. Consensus does not extend past FY2030 at all, so the entire cliff is outside the published forecast horizon. Complicating it, a cheap biosimilar pembrolizumab backbone arrives three years before Imfinzi's own date (Section 4.2).

7. $59bn of goodwill and intangibles against $50bn of equity, tested at the level of one segment against the share price. Goodwill of $21,242m plus other intangibles of $37,846m. Section 10.4 sets out why the segment-level test cannot fail while market capitalisation exceeds book equity, and why write-downs appear only at product level. The current reading: $345m of intangible impairment in Q2 2026 alone against $218m for all of FY2025.

8. The Reported profit and loss is diverging from the Core basis on which guidance is set. Q2 2026 Reported operating profit −10% actual and −13% CER while Core rose 12%; Reported EPS −2% CER while Core EPS rose 18% CER; depreciation, amortisation and impairment +39% to $1,928m. Section 13.3 has the quarter, Section 14 the consensus treatment and the IFRS 18 re-categorisation landing 1 January 2027.

9. Customer concentration: two wholesalers are 25.5% of group Product Sales and three are about 78% of US sales. Two individually exceeded 10% of Product Sales in FY2025 at $8,218m and $5,957m, against one at $7,567m in FY2024 and one at $6,513m in FY2023; the three-wholesaler share has moved 80%, 74%, 78% across the three years. There is no minimum purchase, no exclusivity and no term commitment on either side, and the three national distributors are not substitutable.

10. Partnered economics: four of the fastest-growing revenue lines are not fully owned, and one partner is now in arbitration. Alliance Revenue was $3,067m in FY2025 growing 38% CER and $1,699m in H1 2026 growing 29% CER, against +5% CER for Product Sales. Daiichi Sankyo owns and manufactures Enhertu and Datroway; Amgen manufactures Tezspire and books the US sale; AstraZeneca manufactures Beyfortus and sells it to Sanofi, against whom it commenced International Chamber of Commerce arbitration in June 2026 over alleged non-performance, with Sanofi counterclaiming. Management declined to comment on the Q2 2026 call. Beyfortus was −37% CER in Q2 2026 on "Partner's adjustment of inventory levels", which is a partner-inventory artefact inside a revenue caption.

11. Litigation and investigations: eight live government matters, and the one with a criminal charge is in China. Beyond the China matters:

  • A June 2024 subpoena from the US Attorney's Office in Boston seeking documents on payments to healthcare providers.
  • A 340B qui tam False Claims Act action under appeal.
  • A 340B antitrust class action revived by the Second Circuit in August 2025.
  • AstraZeneca's own constitutional challenges to the 340B statutes of 21 states. It has lost or been denied relief in six, and in Arkansas has been ordered to pause its contract-pharmacy policy.
  • A Soliris end-payor antitrust class action alleging improper patents delayed biosimilar entry, partially dismissed in December 2025.
  • A Novartis Lanham Act suit filed October 2025 over AstraZeneca's paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria marketing statements.
  • The Syntimmune adverse determinations of $311m.
  • The Definiens earn-out arbitration, unresolved twelve years on.

FY2025 added a standalone anti-bribery and anti-corruption principal risk naming the UK Bribery Act, the UK Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act and the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act — a risk factor that appeared in the same year its underlying event was indicted.

12. Balance sheet and financing: net debt up $3,538m in six months against a rising deal cadence. Covered in Section 12. The ranked items are investment spending rather than refinancing, commercial paper reliance on a three-year-old short-term rating with an undisclosed programme size, the $144m-a-year step-up on the 2028–2030 low-coupon tranche, structural subordination of the guaranteed notes, and a floating-rate sensitivity whose sign has flipped.

13. Supply, quality and manufacturing concentration behind an unnamed supply base. No active-pharmaceutical-ingredient supplier and no contract manufacturer is named anywhere in the filings (Section 5.3). Until the supply base is established, the concentration and geographic exposure of the small-molecule input base cannot be assessed at all, and the "substantially all US-made" commitment cannot be tested for feasibility. The one technical constraint the filings do not address and that would determine whether a $2.2bn purchase converts to revenue is actinium-225 supply and radiopharmacy distribution for the Fusion radioconjugates, where the Pluvicto supply constraints are the precedent.

14. Cyber, data and artificial intelligence, entirely qualitative. Artificial intelligence went from 1 mention in the FY2021 risk factors to 20 in FY2025 and 53 across the FY2025 report, and the risk text is entirely qualitative, with no spend figure, no dependency and no measurable exposure.

15. Governance items to watch. CEO succession in a fourteenth year with disclosure limited to "desktop research relating to potential external candidates"; a pay-policy renewal due at the 2027 AGM against an 18.4% benchmarked shortfall; a pay plan with zero weight on returns, margin, net debt or share count; and the one non-independent director's attendance record on the two committees that validate 30% of the bonus and 40% of the long-term award.

These risks are correlated. A single quarter could combine the Farxiga and Lynparza erosion curves running together (Risk 1), the Calquence Maximum Fair Price landing 1 January 2027 (Risk 2), a further step in the US gross-to-net rate (Risk 3), continued Chinese procurement (Risk 4) and one of the two H2 2026 readouts failing (Risk 5) — and the first four of those are the same mechanism, price, arriving through four different channels. They would appear together in the gross margin, which alliance-revenue mix has been holding up.

19. Source disclosure

Sources.

  • SEC XBRL company facts (ifrs-full, CIK 0000901832, FY2015–FY2025, complete with no year gap across 13 line items), plus the same for 16 peers on us-gaap and ifrs-full.
  • AstraZeneca's own filings and disclosures: 10 Annual Report exhibits (FY2016–FY2025), 5 full 20-F wrappers (FY2021–FY2025), 10 quarterly 6-Ks (2024-Q1 to 2026-Q2), 43 earnings-call transcripts gap-free from 2015Q4 to 2026Q2, 44 presentation and event transcripts from 2016 to 2026, and 19 investor decks with 1,029 slides.
  • The Bloomberg terminal.
  • Peer and value-chain filings for McKesson, Cencora, Cardinal Health, CVS, Cigna, UnitedHealth, Alexion (pre-acquisition), and the 20-Ks and 20-Fs of the named pharmaceutical peers.
  • CMS administrative datasets for Medicare Part D, Part B and Medicaid spending by drug.

Gaps and failures.

  • No sell-side research on AstraZeneca. External-consensus framing comes from Bloomberg and from named published notes retrieved from the web.
  • No proxy statement, because AstraZeneca is a foreign private issuer. Executive pay is disclosed in the Directors' Remuneration Report inside the Annual Report and in 20-F Items 6 and 11. Section 16 does not apply, so no Form 4 insider-transaction record exists; the only director-dealing record is the annual beneficial-interest table plus regulatory-news notifications.
  • No franchise profitability anywhere. One reportable segment under IFRS 8. Every franchise margin, return and invested-capital figure in this dossier is an estimate with its method stated.
  • No quarterly consensus exists for this filer on Bloomberg, so standalone-quarter revenue and earnings surprises are not recoverable, and three of the twelve reporting events (the 2023, 2024 and 2025 half-years) have no stored consensus.
  • No estimate dispersion. Every Bloomberg high, low and standard-deviation field for forward earnings returned empty for every fiscal year, so multiple ranges implied by dispersion cannot be given; contributor counts are reported instead.
  • No consensus operating cash flow or free cash flow. Those two lines in Section 13.1 are blank rather than filled from the model.
  • AstraZeneca files no 10-K, so the risk-factor comparison in Section 18 uses Item 3.D of each 20-F and covers FY2021–FY2025 only, because the earlier wrappers incorporate risk factors by reference.
  • Two external datasets were pulled on 7 August 2026: openFDA approval events and clinicaltrials.gov trial starts. See Appendix C.
  • Daloopa has no AstraZeneca coverage; XBRL substitutes.
  • Two CMS pages returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so the Farxiga Maximum Fair Price figures come from secondary sources and are tagged [web, unverified].

Discrepancy log. The as-filed IFRS figure wins on every income-statement, balance-sheet and cash-flow line. Bloomberg's operating profit differs from the filing by −$150m to +$216m across the eleven years with the sign flipping, which is a re-standardisation of the "Other operating income and expense" line rather than one rule. Bloomberg's operating cash flow is higher in all eleven years because AstraZeneca classifies interest received within investing activities and Bloomberg puts it in operating; the FY2023–FY2025 differences of $287m, $343m and $286m are inside those years' finance income. Net debt reconciles exactly: the gap to Bloomberg is the net-derivatives line AstraZeneca includes in its own definition, and AstraZeneca's definition itself changed in FY2022 to include lease liabilities, so the FY2015–FY2021 series is on a slightly narrower base. AstraZeneca's disclosed FY2025 EBITDA of $19,476m matches the computed series to the dollar; Bloomberg reports $19,666m, higher by exactly the operating-profit difference. Core operating profit for FY2017, FY2019 and FY2021 differs by 0.2–0.4% between a transcription from the Annual Report Financial Reviews and a back-solve from the following year's disclosed growth rate; the transcribed series is used. Bloomberg's "Earnings EPS" column does not reconcile to reported EPS ($6.9158 against $6.60 basic for 2025) while its "Comparable EPS" matches disclosed Core EPS exactly, so Comparable EPS is used throughout and Earnings EPS discarded. Two China figures exist for FY2025 — $6,654m on the management Total Revenue basis and $6,636m on the Note 2 statutory Product Sales basis, and both are correct on their own basis. Two Farxiga FY2025 figures exist for the same reason: $8,492m of Total Revenue and $8,400m of Product Sales. Two Rare Disease FY2024 figures appear in one annual report, $8,768m and $8,668m, reconciling by a $100m Koselugo collaboration milestone, so FY2025 growth is +4% on one basis and +5% on the other. Three irreconcilable dapagliflozin patient counts exist — "about 77 million patients globally" in the Annual Report, "definitely 60 million patients" molecule-wide on the Q2 2026 call, and 19–32m branded patient-years from triangulation, and none is used as a volume denominator. The Q2 2026 transcript renders Farxiga's decline as "90%" where the 6-K reports −19% CER, a transcription artefact; the filing governs. And a deck slide renders "13¹ manufacturing sites in US" as "131" in the extracted text, which the image resolves.

Unresolved internal inconsistencies.

  • FY2025 Reported return on invested capital appears at three values. 16.0% in the Section 3.2 decade table and the Section 13.1 returns row; 15.6% in the Section 3.2 peer table, the gap table and the prose of Sections 3 and 3.3; and 14.6% described as "goodwill-inclusive" in Section 3.2. The invested-capital bases differ but the document does not state how. The peer comparison and the widening-gap conclusion use 15.6%.
  • The most-recent-quarter peer medians in Section 3.2 do not reproduce from their own columns. Excluding the three peers footnote 3 removes, the median operating margin of the remaining eleven is 31.8% against the 35.0% printed, which would make the AstraZeneca gap −11.2pp rather than −14.4pp, and the median gross margin is 75.2% against 74.7%. The revenue-growth median of about +10% does reproduce. The peer set behind those two cells cannot be recovered from the document.
  • The FY2023 column of the Section 1 franchise table sums to $45,214m against the $45,811m Total Revenue printed in its own total row. The $597m difference is close to FY2023 Collaboration Revenue, so the FY2023 franchise figures appear to be on a Product Revenue basis while FY2024 and FY2025 are Total Revenue. The FY2024 column foots exactly, and the two-year franchise growth rates in Section 6 use the FY2023 figures as printed.
  • The Section 10.3 business-development column sums to $35,486m against the $35,818m total printed, and the free-cash-flow-after-business-development column to $23,139m against $22,807m — the same $332m in both. The printed total is what the $20,708m dividend gap and the Section 10.5 table use, and the row carrying the difference cannot be identified from the document.

  • Section 4.2 credits AstraZeneca with 10 positive Phase III readouts in FY2025 against the 16 in the Section 13.4 KPI table. The Section 4.2 cell may be Oncology-scoped, which its source does not state.

20. What we still don't know, and the monitoring KPIs

20.1 Material gaps

  • Franchise-level profitability exists for one franchise only. Rare Disease can be put at a 43–52% Core operating margin (Section 3.3); Oncology only at a 26–36% assumed band and BioPharmaceuticals only at a direction with no usable magnitude. With one IFRS 8 segment, whether Oncology at 43.6% of revenue earns more or less per dollar than the franchise AstraZeneca paid $39bn for is unanswerable (§3, §11). What would close it: an IFRS 18 recut producing a therapy-area management-defined performance measure from 1 January 2027, or a disclosed research-and-selling split by therapy area. Neither is obligatory.
  • There is no medicine-level revenue history. Individual medicines exist only as FY2025 and H1 2026 cross-sections, so the erosion rates and pipeline-replacement arithmetic in Section 17 have no per-medicine growth track record to calibrate against (§17.2).
  • The geographic history is four years long and China is one year long. Product Sales by geography exist for FY2022–FY2025 only, Total Revenue by region for FY2025 only, and exactly one China row ($6,654m in FY2025). For an exposure that is 11.3% of revenue and the sharpest inflection in the business, there is no basis to judge whether the decline breaks a decade trend or reverts to one (§6.3, §18 Risk 4).
  • The scale of Chinese domestic competition is not established. Whether China's decline is procurement price — volume-preserving, which is management's recovery thesis — or share loss to a domestic third-generation inhibitor or conjugate from Hengrui, Innovent, Akeso, Sino Biopharmaceutical, Junshi or Qilu, which would be permanent, is unresolved on 11.3% of revenue, despite Soriot conceding that Tagrisso and conjugate competition in China is "very, very intense" (§4.3, §17.3).
  • AstraZeneca publishes no dated regulatory and readout calendar. The pipeline bucket in Section 17 therefore applies probabilities to assets with no dated arrival year, and the monitoring list below has no dated catalysts beyond the two H2 2026 readouts.
  • Farxiga has no independent volume-versus-price decomposition. Whether the −18% CER cardio-renal print is price collapse with volume intact or volume loss to generics matters most, and Sections 1, 6 and 17 each take an implicit position on it.
  • The $3,138m increase in US managed-care and Medicare rebates is never split between Part D redesign mechanics (a one-time 2025 reset), the Farxiga Maximum Fair Price (permanent and product-specific) and pharmacy-benefit-manager rebate escalation (recurring). The three have completely different persistence, so identical FY2025 facts imply different FY2027–FY2030 net-price paths.
  • AstraZeneca does not split the gross-margin gain between alliance mix and underlying cost. The mechanism is disclosed and the FY2025 Financial Review names the profit-share drag in the same table where Gross Margin rose. With Alliance Revenue at $3,067m and the caption itself redefined effective 1 January 2025, Section 13's margin narrative and the mid-30s target are judged against a trend that may be substantially a mix effect on a changed base.
  • The return consequence of the $50bn US onshoring commitment is nowhere disclosed. The incremental depreciation, the utilisation the capacity needs and the return drag on a business earning 82% gross margins with most active-ingredient manufacture outsourced are absent, against a tariff exemption expiring around late 2028. Section 17 models research and selling as revenue percentages with no separate onshoring depreciation step.
  • Who manufactures the medicines is not disclosed. AstraZeneca names no active-pharmaceutical-ingredient supplier and no contract manufacturer, so a single-source dependency on a critical active ingredient or a biologics fill-finish site can neither be ruled in nor out. Section 5.3's conclusion about the binding constraint is untested.
  • The quarterly series starts FY2023Q3. FY2020–FY2022, where the roughly $4bn of COVID-19 revenue and the Alexion integration step-up fall, has no quarterly view, so every seasonality statement depends on three years.
  • The first-appearance dates for exclusivity, China and pricing language in the risk factors are not established, because the FY2016–FY2020 20-F wrappers incorporate risk factors by reference — the cheapest available evidence on whether management saw each risk coming.
  • AstraZeneca discloses no R&D-productivity measure. The only quantified disclosure is from the 2014 Investor Day: cost per candidate drug $50–60m against an $80–110m industry benchmark, and probability of success up from about 6% to about 16% since 2010. Nothing since discloses cost per candidate or phase-transition probability, so the reinvestment-runway test on the company's own named binding constraint cannot be applied to $14.2bn of annual spend.
  • Three things that bear directly on AstraZeneca are unknown from its own disclosure: the Enhertu and Datroway split economics with Daiichi Sankyo, the pace of Keytruda's 2028 exclusivity loss and subcutaneous conversion, which sets Imfinzi's competitive frame, and Soliris biosimilar uptake, which sets the Rare Disease erosion rate.
  • Three questions the filings do not answer are unresolved: who won the batch-11 Chinese tender volume and at what price, how US oncology prescribers choose between Imfinzi and Keytruda, and how fast infusion centres switch Soliris patients to Ultomiris rather than to a biosimilar.

20.2 Open questions still outstanding

Ranked by importance:

  • What Core operating margin does management now expect for FY2026, after the target went unmentioned on both 2026 calls?
  • What phasing gets +5% CER in Q2 to the reconfirmed full-year band?
  • What risk-adjustment factor is inside the $80bn, and how large are the "Loss of Exclusivity" and "IRA impact" bars in the bridge, which every version marks "illustrative only, not to scale"?
  • What is the dollar most-favoured-nation headwind inside FY2026 guidance?
  • What net-price reduction does Calquence's $8,600 Maximum Fair Price represent, given no party discloses its current Part D net price?
  • What is the capital-expenditure-versus-research split of the $50bn US commitment, and its annual profile?
  • Under what conditions would the 2012 buyback suspension be lifted, and what is the intended steady-state payout ratio?
  • What is the size and cost of the commercial paper programme?
  • What is AstraZeneca's realised Phase II-to-III and Phase III success rate, and what does the "75% plus" record refer to?
  • What are ex-US units and realised price? No public administrative dataset gives per-brand units for China, the EU or Japan, so 54% of oncology Product Sales cannot be decomposed at all.
  • What is the exact base on which the Daiichi Sankyo profit share is computed, and what are the collaboration's term, renewal and termination provisions?
  • What is the revenue at risk from the 2028 Part B change?
  • What share of the $2,681m fair-value-through-other-comprehensive-income receivable balance is Chinese bank acceptance drafts?
  • Will IFRS 18 produce a franchise-level subtotal? That would partly lift the constraint forcing every franchise margin in this dossier to be an estimate.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

Nineteen decks and 1,029 slides span November 2014 to July 2026. Eleven add something the filings and transcripts do not.

  • The $80bn bridge, its base year and its currency basis are deck-only. The ambition itself appears in the FY2025 Annual Report, but the bridge behind it does not: base year, minus a named "Loss of Exclusivity" bucket (Brilinta, Farxiga, Lynparza, Soliris), minus a named "IRA impact" bucket, plus 13 to 14 named existing medicines, plus 15 to 18 named launching new medicines. Every version is marked "Illustrative only, not to scale" with no figures. The base moved from $45.8bn (2023) to $54.1bn (2024) and back with the endpoint fixed, so the implied rate has been 9.7%, 6.7% and now 6.4%. And the financial ambitions are footnoted "based on Q1 2024 exchange rates", deck-only. [Investor Day 2024, slide 8; H1 2025 results, slide 32; FY2025 results, slide 13] → §14, §17.6
  • The mid-30s% Core operating margin target exists only in the decks. "On track to achieve mid-30s% Core operating margin by 2026… Beyond 2026… the Company will target at least mid-30s%", restated at the FY2025 results as "Targeting mid-30%s Core operating margin" with the same FX footnote. The string "mid-30" is deck-only. The named mechanism is testable and one item of it is unusual: "Greater speciality mix · LCMs leveraging existing commercial model · LOEs enabling resource redeployment · Optimising global footprint". The exclusivity wave is presented as a source of margin. [Investor Day 2024 CFO deck, slides 7, 11, 12] → §7, §8, §14
  • Per-asset non-risk-adjusted peak-year revenue is a deck-only forecast layer. The decks publish asset-level guidance in two buckets, latest at eleven asset groups above $5bn (wholly owned conjugates, volrustomig, rilvegostomig, saruparib, the CAR-T, surovatamig, camizestrant, the baxdrostat franchise, the dapagliflozin combinations, the laroprovstat franchise and the weight-management franchise) and six at $3–5bn (tozorakimab, sonesitatug vedotin, two dapagliflozin combinations, cliramitug, efzimfotase alfa). Management states they cannot be summed; its own aggregations are separate and risk-adjusted at "about $20bn potential revenue in 2030" from the 2024–2025 readouts and "additional combined risk-adjusted more than $10bn" from the 2026 cohort. [H1 2026 results, slide 25; FY2025 results, slides 5, 27, 33] → §17.3
  • Pipeline value density, deck-only. Unique assets in Phase III plus registration went 27, 30, 33, 37, 37 across 2021–2025 while average non-risk-adjusted peak-year revenue per late-stage indication went from about $600m to about $1,290m. An earlier version of the slide counted trials rather than assets: 81, 77, 84, 91 late-stage trials with average peak revenue passing $1bn. Companion counts, all deck-only at this granularity: 272 trials in the pipeline and 104 in Phase III as of 6 November 2025; 57,000 then 61,000 patients in active trials excluding the Alexion pipeline. [JPM 2026, slides 7–8; JPM 2025, slide 20] → §2, §17.3
  • The magnitude of what the buyback suspension gave up is visible only in the 2014 deck (§10.5, and the slide below), under a framework of "R&D · Business Development · Progressive dividend policy · Efficient capital structure". Every framework slide since 2020 has four priorities and none is a buyback, and nothing has been repurchased in the fourteen years since. [Investor Day 2014, slides 7, 13; Alexion deck 2020, slide 22; Investor Day 2024 CFO deck, slide 9; JPM 2026, slide 16] → §10.5
  • The only quantified R&D-productivity disclosure in the entire archive is eleven years old. The 2014 deck states research and early-development spend reduced 39% and headcount 42% since 2010, back-up programmes cut from 48% of the portfolio to under 2%, plus the cost-per-candidate and probability-of-success figures set out in §20.1. Nothing in any later deck or filing discloses cost per candidate or a phase-transition probability. [Investor Day 2014, slide 62] → §20.1
  • Artificial intelligence applied to operations is quantified only in the decks: a 50% reduction in synthetic route-design lead time, more than 20% higher manufacturing yield at one Swedish site, a 90% reduction in dispensing planning time, and "potential to reduce CMC development time for synthetic manufacturing to commercial scale by 50%". [H1 2023 results, slide 13; JPM 2026, slide 9] → §2
  • The Rare Disease patient series was published once and shows realised price declining (§8). Alongside it, the gMG treatment funnel (72,000 diagnosed antibody-positive US patients narrowing to 66,000, 36,000 and 9,000 by line), diagnosed populations by indication, and a forecast that branded medicines reach about 80% of the gMG market by 2034 from 25–30% today. [Investor Day 2024, slides 79, 82–86, 93] → §8, §20.1
  • Lung-franchise and hypertension market shares, deck-only. FLAURA 73%, PACIFIC 67% and ADAURA 67% US market share on internal estimates; Tagrisso above 75% of third-generation inhibitors prescribed globally on IQVIA data to May 2026. And the distribution case for baxdrostat: more than 20m US and more than 75m ex-US uncontrolled second-line-plus hypertension patients, about 85% managed in primary care, more than 90% of cardiologists already reached, with the first two footnoted as US-scoped internal estimates. [Investor Day 2024, slide 18-equivalent; H1 2026 results, slide 14; ESC 2025, slides 24, 28] → §3, §4.2
  • The conjugate platform map colour-codes ownership, showing Enhertu and Datroway as alliance assets against seven wholly owned and five proprietary-platform conjugates, which makes visible that the mix shift moves conjugate revenue from an alliance gross-profit share to full Product Sales — and therefore from roughly 100% reported gross margin to full cost of goods. [ESMO 2025, slide 25] → §2, §17.3
  • The Alexion deck disclosed the entire exclusivity wave five years early, with US patent expiry for 19 products from Brilinta around 2024 and Farxiga around 2025 through Tagrisso and Calquence around 2031 to Ultomiris in 2035, alongside the target's 20% revenue compound rate 2017 to 2020 and the claim that about 70% of paroxysmal-nocturnal-haemoglobinuria patients switched off Soliris within 18 months. [Alexion deck 2020, slides 7, 10] → §3.1, §11.1

The datasets report beneficiaries, dosage units and total spending per brand per year, which is the volume-times-price decomposition the filings do not give.

§1.1 — Farxiga's Medicare Maximum Fair Price. cms.gov, accessed 2026-08-07 [web, unverified]. The negotiated price is $178.50 per 30-day supply effective 1 January 2026, a 68% discount to the 2023 list price of $556. Both CMS pages returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so the figures are taken from search-result summaries and corroborated across secondary reports; treat the $178.50 / $556 / 68% triple as high confidence and anything more granular as unverified.

§1.1 — Calquence's Maximum Fair Price. Simon-Kucher, accessed 2026-08-07. CMS announced the fifteen 2027 negotiated prices on 25 November 2025; Calquence's Maximum Fair Price is $8,600 per 30-day supply, about 41% below the $14,486 list price.

Tagrisso $17,117.30 per 30 tablets, or $570.58 per tablet (goodrx.com, accessed 2026-08-07); Calquence $14,485.92 per 30-day supply, $241.43 per tablet, and Lynparza $15,886.92 per 30-day supply, $132.39 per tablet (drugs.com price guides, accessed 2026-08-07); Fasenra $6,022.46 per 30mg dose; Tezspire $4,587.41 per 210mg syringe; Breztri $665 per 30-day supply. CMS gross unit prices land at 97–103% of list in every case tested, which is what makes the administrative data usable as a list-price index.

AI-discovered molecules achieve 80–90% Phase I success, well above historic averages, but only about 40% in Phase II, in line with history; a 2025 Nature Medicine paper found Phase II failure rates "similar" to non-AI drugs; and roughly $60bn has flowed into AI drug discovery since 2019, producing about 175 clinical-stage programmes and no approvals.

§2 and §17 — Published phase-transition base rates. bio.org, accessed 2026-08-07, the BIO / Informa Pharma Intelligence / QLS Advisors dataset of 12,728 phase transitions across 9,704 programmes and 1,779 companies, 2011–2020. Overall likelihood of approval from Phase I 7.9%; all oncology 5.3%; solid tumours 4.6%; biologics 9.1%; and programmes using patient-preselection biomarkers 15.9% against 7.6% without.

Appendix C — External data sources

Two external datasets were pulled on 7 August 2026, both from free public APIs. The supporting workpapers are workpapers\edge-openfda_approvals.md and workpapers\edge-clinicaltrials_starts.md, and workpapers\edge_prep_azn.py reproduces every figure below. Figures from these sources are cited [data: <dataset>, pull 2026-08-07].

The two datasets aim at the same gap §20.1 records as unclosed: AstraZeneca discloses no R&D-productivity measure, and the only quantified productivity disclosure it has published is from the 2014 Investor Day. The two point in opposite directions. Against the peer cohort, AstraZeneca converts research spend into late-stage trials and into FDA approval events more efficiently than most of the mega-caps. Against its own history, both ratios have roughly halved since 2020 while research spend grew 137%.

openFDA drug approvals — pulled 7 August 2026 from https://api.fda.gov/drug/drugsfda.json (drugs@FDA, source last_updated 7 August 2026). Period covered: 1951 to 7 August 2026, with the analysis covering 2006 to 2026. 110 applications and 266 approved submissions.

drugs@FDA stores sponsor_name as an untokenized keyword, so a query for ASTRAZENECA matches only the 80 applications filed under that exact string and drops Imfinzi, Fasenra, Tezspire, Saphnelo, Beyfortus, Wainua and every Alexion medicine. The wildcard family sponsor_name:ASTRAZENECA* OR sponsor_name:ALEXION* OR sponsor_name:MEDIMMUNE* returns all 110, spread across eight stored spellings: ASTRAZENECA (80), ASTRAZENECA AB (20), ALEXION PHARM (4), ASTRAZENECA LP (2), and one each of ASTRAZENECA PHARMS, ASTRAZENECA UK LTD, ALEXION PHARMS INC and MEDIMMUNE ONCOLOGY. Querying the exact string alone would have under-counted by 27%.

Original approvals are the wrong metric for this portfolio: they run at one to six a year and ten of the 32 since 2015 are new formulations, new devices or second applications for a molecule already approved. The output is in efficacy supplements — new indications and label expansions — of which the family holds 187 in total and 118 across 2016 to 2025. Sixty-two of those 118 attach to six brands, led by Imfinzi at 16 and Lynparza at 15 since 2015. AstraZeneca's US approval record over the decade is better described as deepening a narrow set of assets than as launching new ones.

Approval events (original NDA/BLA + efficacy supplements) 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025
Original NDA/BLA approvals 1 2 2 4 5 1 1
Efficacy supplements 24 17 8 11 5 17 11
R&D expense, $bn 6.1 6.0 9.7 9.8 10.9 13.6 14.2
Events per $bn R&D 4.1 3.2 1.0 1.5 0.9 1.3 0.8

Across 2016 to 2025 cumulatively, AstraZeneca produced 1.63 approval events per $bn of research spend on $87.9bn spent. That places it upper-middle of the twelve-company cohort: behind AbbVie at 1.97 and Amgen at 1.69, level with Novartis at 1.63, and roughly 60% ahead of Merck & Co (1.03), Roche (1.02), Pfizer (1.01), Eli Lilly (0.99) and Johnson & Johnson (0.96). No company in the cohort clears 2.0.

Limitations. sponsor_name is the current application holder rather than the sponsor at the time of approval, so the database is a snapshot of today's ownership projected backwards: Synagis, once MedImmune's largest product, now appears under SWEDISH ORPHAN and is absent from AstraZeneca's history entirely, while Alexion's Soliris (2007), Strensiq (2015), Kanuma (2015) and Ultomiris (2018) are attributed to AstraZeneca in years before the July 2021 acquisition. Peer families inherit the same defect in proportion to how much each company has transacted, and three peer families needed manual repair (Merck KGaA excluded from Merck & Co, Eli Lilly split across two prefixes, Pfizer dominated by Hospira generics). Approval counts say nothing about the commercial value of an approval. The data are US-only, so the EU, Japan and China are absent and China is 11.3% of revenue. And approval dates lag the research that produced them by five to ten years, so the per-dollar ratio divides today's output by today's spend and mismatches the two by most of a decade; the direction of the series is informative and the level in any single year is not.

clinicaltrials.gov trial starts — pulled 7 August 2026 from https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies (API v2). Period covered: 1994 to 7 August 2026, with the phase analysis covering 2012 to 2026. 3,995 studies under the AstraZeneca family as lead sponsor, of which 2,970 are interventional.

The registry's query.spons parameter matches collaborators as well as lead sponsors, so a plain query returns 4,783 studies including investigator-sponsored work in which AstraZeneca only supplied drug. Restricting to AREA[LeadSponsorName](AstraZeneca OR Alexion OR MedImmune) returns 3,995 across five spellings: AstraZeneca (3,467), MedImmune LLC (270), Alexion Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (254), AstraZeneca Turkey (3) and MedImmune Ltd (1). Unlike drugs@FDA, the registry does not rewrite a lead sponsor on acquisition, so Alexion's trials stay under their own name whether they started in 2014 or 2025. Including them gives one consistent basis across the whole period, at the cost of attributing 7 to 22 pre-2021 phased starts a year to AstraZeneca; the size of that attribution is disclosed by year in edge-clinicaltrials_starts_series.csv.

Interventional trial starts by phase 2016 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025
Phase I 35 39 49 52 45 32 48 44
Phase II 14 16 37 20 24 22 30 40
Phase III 14 27 35 35 28 35 36 29
Phase III as % of phased starts 22.2% 32.9% 28.9% 32.7% 28.9% 39.3% 31.6% 25.7%
Phase III starts per $bn R&D 2.38 4.46 5.84 3.59 2.87 3.20 2.65 2.04

Phase III activity is not falling in absolute terms: it has run 28 to 36 a year every year since 2020, and the partial 2026 year already shows 27 starts by 7 August. But the late-stage share peaked at 39.3% in 2023 and has since rotated back to mid-stage, with Phase II starts reaching 40 in 2025, the highest in the fifteen years covered. The 2023 late-stage peak fills the 2026 to 2028 readout calendar; the 2025 mid-stage build fills Phase III in 2027 to 2028 and approvals from 2030.

Across 2016 to 2025 cumulatively AstraZeneca started 287 Phase III studies and 1,018 interventional studies, more than any company in the twelve-company cohort, on the fifth-largest research budget. At 3.27 Phase III starts per $bn of research spend it ranks first, ahead of AbbVie (2.79), Novartis (2.77), Eli Lilly (2.70) and Sanofi (2.65), and roughly 2.5x Roche (1.33) and Johnson & Johnson (1.23). Against Roche and Merck & Co, which spent $147bn and $143bn, AstraZeneca started 46% and 15% more Phase III studies on $88bn. The trend also separates the cohort: AstraZeneca's annual interventional starts went 69 in 2016 to 121 in 2025, while Johnson & Johnson went 99 to 33, GSK 151 to 43 and Novartis 102 to 59.

The registry gives the dated readout calendar §20.1 says is missing. Of 186 ongoing Phase III studies, 113 have a primary completion date on or after August 2026 — 12 in the remainder of 2026, 37 in 2027, 29 in 2028, 20 in 2029, 10 in 2030 and 5 in 2031 to 2033, with combined enrolment of 130,138 participants. Fifty-seven are oncology and 56 are not, and eight of the ten largest by enrolment are outside oncology: AZURE-Outcomes (15,100 participants, AZD0780, primary completion October 2029), Prevent-HF (11,300, baxdrostat/dapagliflozin, December 2029), THARROS (5,250, Breztri in COPD, December 2027), BaxDuo-Pacific (5,000, December 2029), BalanceD-HF (4,800, June 2027), Embold (4,500, elecoglipron in weight management, July 2028), TILIA (3,527, tozorakimab, November 2027) and AZURE-LDL (3,103, January 2027). The full 113 rows, with trial identifier, acronym, status, enrolment, conditions and interventions, are in workpapers\edge-clinicaltrials_phase3_calendar.csv. Those 113 also corroborate a self-reported figure: management disclosed 104 assets in Phase III on 6 November 2025, and the two agree once the 73 studies already past their primary analysis and open only for follow-up are excluded.

Limitations. A trial start is a crude proxy for research output: it weights a 12-patient gefurulimab study identically to the 15,100-patient AZURE-Outcomes trial, so a company running fewer and larger trials looks less productive on the same budget. Rising trial size is a sufficient explanation for AstraZeneca's own halving of starts per research dollar since 2020, and this dataset cannot separate that from declining efficiency. Every date in the calendar is the sponsor's own estimate, revises without notice, marks when the primary endpoint is measured rather than when data are released, and refers to the final primary analysis rather than to any pre-specified interim — which is why the monitoring table in §20.3 can list AVANZAR as an H2 2026 readout while the registry's estimated primary completion for that study is 1 November 2027, with both correct. Withdrawn studies are not netted out. Registry coverage is uneven before roughly 2010, so the pre-2012 tail in the CSV should not be read as a trend. The series is not split by geography, so how much recent activity is Chinese regulatory work rather than new global programmes stays open. And the registry records status rather than outcome, so §20.2's question about AstraZeneca's realised Phase II-to-III and Phase III success rates remains unanswered.
